question: We've got 20 council flats getting new kitchens next month. The housing association sent over their management survey for the block. Is that enough or do I need a different survey before we rip the old units out?
reference_answer: A management survey is meant for normal use and routine maintenance and is usually not intrusive into the fabric. Before refurbishment you need a refurbishment survey of the areas being worked on, which is fully intrusive. HSG264 says that where only certain rooms such as kitchens are being upgraded, the refurbishment survey can be limited to those rooms. Where the management survey was not intrusive in the area you will disturb, a refurbishment survey is required.
label_note: para 50: refurbishment survey needed where the management survey was not intrusive; para 41: can be limited to rooms upgraded, eg kitchens; para 51: refurb survey is fully intrusive

question: No survey, no register, nothing for this tenant's flat. Housing officer says just get on with the bathroom. Can we start?
reference_answer: No. Before work that could expose your men, the law says you must either check whether asbestos is there (type, material, condition) or, if unsure, treat it as present and not just white asbestos, and apply the rules. The ACOP says a survey with sample analysis may be needed, or you treat the material as blue or brown asbestos and bring in a licensed contractor where required. Sheet a0 says do not start work without a clear survey or register.
label_note: reg 5: assess or presume asbestos (not chrysotile alone) before work; L143 148-149 and sheet a0 have no finished tree | relabel: added 3 key(s) from now-parsed hse-asbestos-a0, hse-l143

question: The survey report says 'no access' for the loft hatch area and the void behind the bath. What does that mean for my lads?
reference_answer: Areas the surveyor could not get into count as having asbestos in them, unless strong evidence shows otherwise. The report should name them, and no maintenance or other work that could disturb them should happen there until they have been checked. A refurbishment survey must go into any areas marked 'no access' last time.
label_note: para 49: areas not accessed presumed to contain asbestos, no work there until checked; App 1 para 5: refurb survey must access previous no-access areas

question: Refurb survey was done in May, the job got pushed back and we're only starting now in November. Anything I should be asking the client about?
topic: delay between refurbishment survey and works
reference_answer: Refurbishment surveys usually skip a condition check because the asbestos is meant to come out soon after. If the gap is long, for example over three months, HSG264 says the client should get a material assessment done and manage the materials in the meantime, with repairs or other action where needed.
label_note: para 124: gap over three months needs a material assessment and interim management

question: How do you actually score an asbestos material? What are the things you add up?
reference_answer: HSG264 adds up four scores: what kind of product it is, how damaged it is, its surface treatment, and which asbestos type it is. Each gets 1 to 3, and damage and surface treatment can also get 0, so totals run from 2 to 12. If nobody has analysed it, score the type as crocidolite (3) unless good evidence says otherwise.
label_note: four parameters (para 125), scores 1-3, nil for two, total 2-12, presumed scored as crocidolite (para 126)

question: Painted AIB ceiling tile in a hallway, a couple of scratches on it, nobody's sampled it. What would that score and is it bad?
reference_answer: Using HSG264 Appendix 4: AIB as a product = 2, a few scratches counts as low damage = 1, AIB with its face painted = 1, and since it has not been analysed the type is scored as crocidolite = 3. That gives 7, which sits in the 7 to 9 band: medium potential for fibre release when disturbed.
label_note: Appendix 4 table: AIB 2, low damage 1, painted AIB 1; para 126: presumed = crocidolite 3; para 127: 7-9 is medium

question: The boiler house lagging scored highest on the survey, so that's the one the client has to deal with first, right?
reference_answer: Not necessarily. The material score only shows which items release fibres most easily. Priority for action comes from a separate priority (risk) assessment that looks at things like location, extent, how the area is used, how many people are there and how often maintenance happens. HSG227 gives the example that a little-used boiler house can end up with a similar overall score to an office used every day, and the dutyholder has to make the judgement.
label_note: material score is not priority; a priority assessment decides; HSG227 App 3 para 8 has the boiler house vs office example

question: These flats were built in 2003. Do we still have to bother about asbestos before we drill?
reference_answer: HSG264 lists construction after 1999 as a reason to conclude a material is unlikely to contain asbestos, since nearly all asbestos products were banned by then. HSE's worker guide says the risk is higher in buildings built or refurbished before 2000. You still have a duty under regulation 5 to assess, so check the build date is reliable and that no older materials were reused.
cited_clauses: hse-asbestos-workers (You are also more likely to be at risk if)
hse-asbestos-a0 page 1 (Why is asbestos a problem?)
label_note: para 38: post-1999 construction as evidence of no asbestos; workers page: built or refurbished before 2000; reg 5 duty to assess | relabel: added 1 key(s) from now-parsed hse-asbestos-a0

question: One of the lads found some grey board above the ceiling in a riser that looks dodgy. He hasn't touched it. What's the procedure?
reference_answer: Stop straight away, sign the area and keep people out. Tell the person in charge and get a sample tested. If the result is negative, carry on; if positive, work out whether a licensed contractor is needed. Or you can treat it as the worst type of asbestos and use the matching controls. Let the client know so their asbestos management plan gets updated.
label_note: only the workers page (stop work, speak to employer) is parsed; EM1 (the real answer) and L143 179 have no finished tree | relabel: added 2 key(s) from now-parsed hse-asbestos-em1, hse-l143 (flow chart figure has no text, left missing)

question: Lad drilled through a panel under a window before checking, there's dust on his sleeves and on the floor, tenant's in the next room. What do I do right now?
reference_answer: Treat it as an uncontrolled release. Warn anyone who could be affected (including the tenant), keep out everyone not needed, find the cause and get control back. Anyone not wearing RPE should leave the area; the worker with a little dust should stay put, damp-wipe outer clothing and remove it, and contaminated clothing and rags go as asbestos waste. Do not sweep. Clean up using the right method, and record the event.
label_note: reg 15(1): mitigate, restore, inform, keep others out; the practical steps (L143 368-369, EM1) have no finished tree | relabel: added 3 key(s) from now-parsed hse-asbestos-em1, hse-l143 (flow chart figure has no text, left missing)

question: After that incident, the lad who drilled wasn't wearing a mask. Do I have to write that down anywhere?
reference_answer: Yes. The ACOP says that where someone was without proper RPE or may have breathed fibres during an incident, you must note the exposure on their health record, or on their personal file if they have no health record. EM1 also says to log the incident.
label_note: no parsed section holds the answer; L143 370 and EM1 have no finished tree | relabel: added 1 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143 (flow chart figure has no text, left missing)

question: A bit of AIB got knocked off a cupboard panel, couple of chunks on the floor. Do I need to get a licensed firm in just to clear that up?
reference_answer: Probably not. Clearing up a small release of AIB that is in fairly intact, separate pieces will probably not need a licensed firm, and the same goes for firmly bound materials like asbestos cement. Releases of lagging, loose fill, sprayed coatings, a big release of AIB, or anything that could reach the control limit need a licensed contractor. Follow the Asbestos essentials clean-up methods. Review note: HSE's asbestos locations page lists AIB debris under higher-risk work for a licensed contractor, so treat debris as licensed work unless a risk assessment under L143 clearly shows otherwise.
label_note: NNLW page: cleaning small quantities of debris is non-licensed, significant quantities licensable; no mention of AIB pieces; L143 366-367 and EM1 have no finished tree | review: wrong_answer fixed (dev-review.jsonl) | relabel: added 3 key(s) from now-parsed hse-asbestos-em1, hse-l143

question: Can my plumbers take off the old lagging on the pipes in the airing cupboard if they're careful and wear masks?
reference_answer: No. Removing or disturbing asbestos pipe lagging is licensable work, so only an HSE-licensed contractor can do it. HSE rates lagging among the worst materials because it gives off fibres very easily. Masks do not change this.
cited_clauses: hse-asbestos-workers (Work that must be carried out by a licensed contractor)
label_note: workers page: you must not work on pipe lagging unless licensed; locations: lagging is high risk, licensed contractor; reg 8(1) licence duty | relabel: added 1 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: The bath panel is AIB, screwed on. We need to get underneath to replace the pipes and then put it back. Licensed job?
topic: removing screwed AIB panel for access
reference_answer: No. Taking off and refitting a loosely fixed (for example screwed) AIB panel to get access for other maintenance, such as pipework under a bath, is given as non-licensed work that is not normally notifiable. It still needs trained workers, a risk assessment, a plan of work and proper controls.
cited_clauses: hse-nnlw (Examples of non-licensed work with asbestos)
label_note: NNLW page lists removal and re-attachment of screwed AIB panels to get under a bath as non-licensed work | relabel: added 2 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: Taking out a small AIB partition in a flat as part of the refurb. Reckon it's about an hour and a half total with two men. What category is that?
reference_answer: Short duration work (under two hours in total, nobody over one hour in seven days) that removes AIB during a refurbishment is normally notifiable non-licensed work: notify, mark out the area, and arrange medicals and health records. If it runs past two hours in total or one man does over an hour, it stops being short duration and needs a licensed contractor.
label_note: minor short duration AIB removal in a refurbishment is NNLW; reg 2(3) defines short duration; AIB work not of short duration is licensable | relabel: added 1 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: Sparky needs to drill through an Artex ceiling to put up a new light. What does he need to do asbestos-wise?
reference_answer: Drilling textured decorative coating to fit fixtures is non-licensed work and not normally notifiable. He must have non-licensed training and use the right method; Asbestos essentials sheet A26 covers drilling into textured coatings.
label_note: drilling textured coatings for fixtures is non-licensed (not NNLW); essentials list names sheet A26 | relabel: added 1 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: Client wants the whole Artex ceiling in the lounge stripped with steamers. Is that something we have to notify?
reference_answer: Yes, normally. Stripping a whole textured ceiling with steam or gel, beyond small areas for fitting smoke alarms or lights, is normally notifiable non-licensed work because the method breaks the material down. Notify before starting, mark out the area, and make sure the workers have medicals and health records.
label_note: large-scale steam or gel removal of textured coatings is NNLW | relabel: added 3 key(s) from now-parsed hse-asbestos-a0, hse-l143

question: After we finish the Artex strip in the enclosure, do I need an analyst to come and give us a clearance certificate?
reference_answer: No. For non-licensable work there is no clearance air test and no independent reoccupation certificate. After big jobs like stripping textured coating, clean the area thoroughly, check it visually, and give the occupier a written statement saying it is clean and fit to use again. HSG248 notes the contractor self-certifies, though a client may ask for a more formal check.
label_note: no parsed section holds the answer; L143 428/465/466 and HSG248 A5.66 have no finished tree | relabel: added 4 key(s) from now-parsed hse-hsg248, hse-l143

question: Row of garages on the estate with cement sheet roofs. We want to take the sheets off whole. Licence, notification, or neither?
reference_answer: Taking asbestos cement sheets off carefully without breaking them, even weathered ones, is non-licensed and not normally notifiable. If the sheets are badly damaged by fire or flood, or the method will smash them, such as dropping the roof, it becomes notifiable non-licensed work. The roof is fragile: nobody should walk on it directly, and you need a safe way of working over it.
label_note: NNLW page: AC sheets removed without breaking (incl weathered) are non-licensed; damaged or dropped roof is NNLW; fragile roof point (L143 281) has no finished tree | relabel: added 4 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: Old vinyl tiles under the kitchen lino, probably asbestos. We're lifting them by hand. Anything special?
reference_answer: Lifting asbestos floor tiles and their adhesive by hand is non-licensed work for trained workers, using the Asbestos essentials method (sheet A23). If the tiles are backed with asbestos paper, or the job will badly break them up, it becomes notifiable non-licensed work. Grinding flooring off needs an HSE-licensed contractor.
label_note: manual removal of tiles and mastic is non-licensed; paper-backed or broken up is NNLW; grinding is licensed; essentials list names A23 | relabel: added 1 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: Do I need a licence to drill a couple of holes in a vinyl floor tile for a pipe?
reference_answer: No licence is needed. HSE lists drilling into an asbestos floor tile as non-licensed, lower-risk work, and maintenance on vinyl and thermoplastic tiles is not normally notifiable. The worker still needs non-licensed training and proper controls; Asbestos essentials sheet A9 covers drilling highly bonded materials.
label_note: drilling a hole in a floor tile is lower-risk non-licensed; maintenance on vinyl tiles is non-licensed; essentials list names A9 | relabel: added 1 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: Tenant wants the Artex off the ceiling, but the ceiling boards underneath are AIB. Can we do it ourselves?
reference_answer: No. HSE lists removal of coatings that cover AIB as higher-risk work for a licensed contractor. The textured coating definition covers only the coating, not the board it sits on, and the board itself may be AIB.
label_note: locations page: removal of coatings covering AIB is licensed work; L143 para 21 has no finished tree | relabel: added 1 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: Fitting a radiator, lad drilled the wall and blue-grey fluffy stuff came pouring out of the cavity. What is it and who deals with it?
reference_answer: That sounds like loose-fill asbestos, which HSE says is likely the worst asbestos material since it is pure asbestos. Stop, get everyone out and follow the accidental release steps. Only an HSE-licensed contractor may work on loose fill, including clearing it up.
label_note: loose fill: blue-grey fluffy, most dangerous, only HSE-licensed contractors; accidental release steps (EM1, L143 366) have no finished tree | relabel: added 3 key(s) from now-parsed hse-asbestos-em1, hse-l143

question: How do I notify NNLW and how much notice do I have to give?
reference_answer: Use HSE's online NNLW form; phone calls and letters are not accepted. Send it before work begins. There is no set notice period and no need to wait for a reply or approval. You get a PDF copy back, which you should keep with the job's plan of work.
label_note: online form only, before work, no minimum notice, no waiting for permission, PDF copy | relabel: added 2 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: We're doing NNLW in tenants' flats. Do I notify the council's environmental health or HSE?
reference_answer: For domestic premises and construction sites the enforcing authority is HSE. Local authorities cover places like shops, offices and hotels. The online form lets you notify any of the regulators.
label_note: table: domestic premises and construction sites are HSE | relabel: added 1 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: We've got Artex strips in 30 flats on the same estate over three months. Do I fill in a notification for every flat?
reference_answer: No. For a longer programme of NNLW jobs in one local area, such as a housing estate, you notify the whole programme in one go.
label_note: a project with multiple NNLW jobs can be notified once | relabel: added 1 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: Two of my lads will be doing notifiable work for the first time. What medicals do they need, who does them, and how often?
reference_answer: Workers new to NNLW need a medical before they start, then at least every three years while they keep doing NNLW. It can be done by an ordinary registered doctor such as a GP, not only an HSE-appointed doctor, and must include a chest examination and lung function test. It is in work time at your cost, and the doctor gives a certificate which you keep for four years.
label_note: NNLW page: before start, every 3 years, GP, chest and lung test, work time, certificate kept 4 years; reg 22(3)-(4) | relabel: added 2 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: The NNLW medical has to be done by one of HSE's own doctors, doesn't it?
reference_answer: No. HSE-appointed doctors are required for licensed work. For NNLW, the medical can be done by a non-appointed registered doctor, for example a local GP. HSE has guidance for doctors doing these checks (MS34).
label_note: NNLW medicals can be done by a GP; reg 2(1) relevant doctor includes a registered practitioner for NNLW; MS34 is the doctors guidance | relabel: added 2 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143, hse-ms34

question: What records do I have to keep for the lads doing NNLW, and for how long?
reference_answer: Each worker needs an entry in a register (health record) giving what asbestos work they did, for how long, and their estimated exposure, plus their medical dates and a way to flag the next one due. Keep it for 40 years. HSE says it can be as basic as noting the workers' names on the notification printout you keep.
label_note: health record contents, 40 years, can be names on the notification copy; reg 22(3) applies 22(1)(a)-(c) to NNLW | relabel: added 2 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: My plasterers and electricians won't be touching asbestos on purpose. Do they still need asbestos training?
reference_answer: Yes. Anyone whose work might disturb the building fabric, and anyone supervising them, needs asbestos awareness training. Plasterers, electricians, plumbers, joiners, decorators and construction workers are all named. The only exception is if you can show they only ever work in buildings with no asbestos.
label_note: awareness training for anyone who could disturb the fabric, trades named; the asbestos-free buildings exception is in L143 (no finished tree) | relabel: added 3 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: Lads have done the awareness course. Can they now remove asbestos floor tiles?
reference_answer: No. Awareness training only helps people avoid asbestos; it does not prepare them to work on it. Anyone who will knowingly disturb asbestos in non-licensed jobs, notifiable or not, needs extra training for that task, covering risk assessment, controls, RPE, waste, emergencies and which work must be notified.
label_note: awareness does not prepare workers to work on asbestos; removing floor tiles needs non-licensable training covering the listed topics | relabel: added 3 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: Training company says the lads' asbestos awareness certificates run out after 12 months and they all have to redo the full course. Is that the law?
reference_answer: No. The law does not require a full formal awareness course to be repeated every 12 months, and a certificate expiry date does not always mean full retraining. Some refreshing is still needed when appropriate, for example e-learning or a talk given in house by a competent manager or supervisor.
cited_clauses: hse-asbestos-training (Refreshing information, instruction and training on asbestos awareness)
label_note: no legal requirement to repeat a full awareness course every 12 months; certificate expiry does not mean full retraining | relabel: added 2 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: How often do the guys doing non-licensed asbestos work need refresher training?
reference_answer: Every year, or sooner if methods or control equipment change, the work changes a lot, or gaps in competence appear. Base it on a training needs analysis; for experienced workers it can be a toolbox talk or online module, with practical parts such as RPE use and decontamination where needed.
cited_clauses: hse-asbestos-training (Refreshing information, instruction and training for licensable and non-licensable work)
label_note: refresher every year or sooner if methods, equipment or work change, or gaps found; based on TNA | relabel: added 3 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: Lads use disposable masks for asbestos jobs. Do they need face fit testing and does it need redoing?
reference_answer: Yes. Tight-fitting facepieces, including disposable masks, need fit testing when first selected, by a competent tester. It must be repeated if they change mask model or size or their face changes a lot (weight change, dental work). Workers need to be clean-shaven for a good seal and should pass a fit test for the exact model and size they use.
cited_clauses: hse-asbestos-workers (What you must do as a worker)
label_note: workers page: pass a face fit test for the specific model and size; when to repeat (L143 304-305) has no finished tree | relabel: added 3 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: Can the lads just sweep up the bits after drilling and bag it with the rest of the rubbish?
reference_answer: No. Never sweep asbestos dust or debris; clean with a Class H vacuum or damp rags. Asbestos waste goes in proper asbestos waste bags (double bagged), kept apart from general rubbish, and must go to a licensed site for disposal.
label_note: workers page: never sweep, use Type H vacuum or wet rags, double-bag waste; disposal at a licensed site (L143 532) has no finished tree | relabel: added 3 key(s) from now-parsed hse-asbestos-a0, hse-l143

question: How should we bag and store the asbestos waste from a non-licensed job until it goes to the tip?
reference_answer: Seal it in suitable labelled bags or wrapping as you go; two plastic sacks are fine for most waste, with tougher packaging for sharp pieces. Do not overfill, and push the air out before sealing. If it is not going straight away, lock the sealed bags in a clearly marked store, for example a lockable skip. Labels must follow the carriage rules or Schedule 2.
label_note: reg 24: sealed, marked receptacles for storing and moving waste; labels per carriage rules or Schedule 2; bagging details (L143 526-528) have no finished tree | relabel: added 4 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: It's only a 20-minute job drilling an AIB panel for a shelf. Do I really need a written plan of work for that?
topic: plan of work for small jobs
reference_answer: Yes. All asbestos work, maintenance included, needs a written plan of work before it starts. It covers what the work is and how long it will take, where it is, the methods, protective and decontamination equipment for workers and others, and the control and cleaning measures, and you keep a copy on site. Keep it in proportion to the job.
label_note: written plan of work for any work with asbestos, its contents, copy kept on site | relabel: added 2 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: Full strip-out of a block of flats. Client wants us to start the joinery while the asbestos removers work alongside us. Allowed?
reference_answer: When a building is being demolished or heavily refurbished, the written plan has to say, where reasonably practicable, that asbestos comes out before other major work starts, unless removal would create more risk than leaving it. HSG264 says removal also makes sense for smaller refurbishments that change the structure or layout.
label_note: remove asbestos before other major works in demolition or major refurbishment; HSG264 para 52 extends this to smaller structural refurbishments | relabel: added 1 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: We're getting a licensed contractor in to strip lagging in the plant room. How much notice do they have to give HSE?
reference_answer: Licensable work has to be notified in writing to the enforcing authority 14 days or more before it starts. The authority can accept less notice (a waiver), for example in an emergency with serious risk. Any significant change must also be notified in writing without delay.
label_note: 14 days in writing, shorter if the authority agrees, material changes without delay | relabel: added 3 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: Our scaffolders are putting up the scaffold for the licensed firm to take off AIB soffits. Do the scaffolders need to be licensed too?
reference_answer: Possibly. Erecting and striking scaffolding to give access for licensable work counts as ancillary work if the scaffolding could foreseeably knock or damage the asbestos. Ancillary work needs a licence whenever the main job is licensable.
label_note: reg 2(2): work with asbestos includes ancillary work; the scaffolding example and licence point (L143 36-38) have no finished tree | relabel: added 2 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: After the licensed removal in the flat, who signs it off as safe for the tenant to move back, and how does that work?
reference_answer: Licensed jobs finish with a four-stage clearance by an independent analyst accredited to ISO 17025: first a check that the work is finished and the site in order, then a detailed visual check inside the enclosure, then an air test, and finally a check once the enclosure has been taken down. If all pass, a reoccupation certificate is issued. For licensed work outdoors, the air test is skipped.
label_note: reg 20(4) only covers the assessor's accreditation; the four-stage clearance (HSG247 7.102/7.105, L143 426-427) has no finished tree | relabel: added 3 key(s) from now-parsed hse-hsg247, hse-l143

question: What air reading does the analyst need to see before the enclosure can come down?
reference_answer: The clearance indicator is 0.01 fibres per ml. After a passed visual inspection, air results must be under this before the area is normally treated as fit to reoccupy. HSG248 notes it only shows the site is clean; it is not a safe long-term level.
label_note: no parsed section holds the answer; HSG247 7.132 and HSG248 6.3 have no finished tree | relabel: added 2 key(s) from now-parsed hse-hsg247, hse-hsg248

question: The removal firm says they'll bring their own analyst for the clearance. Is that OK now, and what's changing in 2027?
reference_answer: Until 25 November 2027 the current regulation 20 applies, so the removal contractor can still appoint an accredited analyst, though HSG248 strongly recommends the building client hires the analyst and says the certificate goes to both. From 25 November 2027 the new regulation 20 bars the employer responsible for the cleaning from appointing whoever assesses it for the reoccupation certificate. That assessor must hold accreditation to both ISO 17020 and 17025.
label_note: new reg 20(3)-(4): cleaning employer cannot appoint the assessor, ISO 17020 and 17025; starts 25 Nov 2027 (reg 1(3)); current reg 20(4) applies until then | relabel: added 2 key(s) from now-parsed hse-hsg248

question: I heard the asbestos rules change on 25 November this year and the removers can't choose their own analyst from next week. Is that right?
reference_answer: Not quite. The 2026 amending regulations mostly start on 25 November 2026, but that part only updates references to other laws. The ban on the cleaning employer appointing the clearance assessor starts on 25 November 2027. Until then the old rules still apply.
label_note: reg 1(2): 25 Nov 2026; reg 1(3): reg 2(2) on 25 Nov 2027; reg 2(3)-(4) only update references; the tree has no Explanatory Note section | relabel: added 0 key(s) from now-parsed

question: Who's responsible for managing asbestos in the stairwells and roof space of the council block, and does that cover inside the flats?
topic: duty to manage in blocks of flats
reference_answer: In blocks of flats, the managing duty reaches the shared areas such as foyers, stairs, lifts, boiler and plant rooms, roof spaces and communal stores. The dutyholder is whoever is responsible for maintenance and repair under the lease or contract, usually the council or housing association. It does not cover the inside of each flat.
cited_clauses: hse-asbestos-duty (What the duty to manage asbestos in buildings is)
label_note: duty covers common parts of multi-occupancy domestic premises such as flats; reg 4(1): dutyholder is whoever has the repair obligation; detail (L143 89, Table 5) has no finished tree | relabel: added 2 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: Housing association says the duty to manage doesn't cover inside the flats, so we're on our own for asbestos info. Does that mean we don't have to check anything inside?
reference_answer: No. The duty to manage does not reach inside private flats, but as the employer you must still check for asbestos before work, or presume it is there and act on that. Landlords also carry general duties under the HSW Act towards people affected by their business. HSE says workers in homes must still be protected.
cited_clauses: hse-asbestos-workers (Workers most likely to come across asbestos)
label_note: reg 5: employer must assess or presume before work; workers page: in homes you must still act | relabel: added 2 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: We're doing repairs in the block's boiler room. The housing association hasn't sent us the asbestos register. Can I insist on it?
reference_answer: Yes. For the common parts, the dutyholder's plan must make sure anyone who might disturb asbestos is told where it is and what state it is in. You also need to check the information is accurate and fits your job, and you have to work with the dutyholder so they can meet their duty.
label_note: reg 4(9)(c): information given to anyone liable to disturb it; reg 4(2): duty to co-operate | relabel: added 2 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: Client says just crack on with the boiler room repairs while they sort out a survey sometime next month. Should we?
topic: stopping work until asbestos is known
reference_answer: No. HSG227 tells dutyholders to stop work that disturbs the fabric straight away until it is known whether asbestos is present, without waiting to arrange a survey, because even small jobs like drilling can release a lot of fibres. As the contractor you must assess or presume asbestos before starting.
label_note: HSG227: stop fabric work immediately, do not wait for a survey; reg 5 for the contractor

question: What's the actual exposure limit for asbestos? I've seen 0.1 and 0.6 mentioned.
reference_answer: The control limit is 0.1 fibres per cm3 averaged over 4 hours. The 0.6 fibres per cm3 figure is a separate peak measured over 10 minutes; exposure above it is not sporadic and low intensity. Going over either points to licensable work.
label_note: reg 2(1): control limit 0.1 f/cm3 over 4 hours; reg 2(4): sporadic and low intensity test, but the 0.6 figure is only in L143 (no finished tree) | relabel: added 3 key(s) from now-parsed hse-l143

question: The refurb has loads of little AIB bits: a panel here, a soffit there, a cupboard lining. Can I treat each one as its own short job so none of it is notifiable?
reference_answer: No. Where several activities on asbestos are part of a bigger job like refurbishing part of a building, they should be looked at together, not one by one, when deciding if the work is NNLW. The short duration test also counts all workers' time over seven days.

reference_answer: Your duties also cover other people affected by your asbestos work, where reasonably practicable. question: Is this asbestos?
reference_answer: I need to know what the material is, where it is, how old the building is, and whether there is a survey or register covering it. You cannot tell asbestos by colour or look alone. The documents say to stop, keep people away, and either get a sample analysed by an accredited lab or presume it is asbestos (and the worst type) and use the right controls.

question: Can we drill here?
reference_answer: It depends on what you are drilling into and whether it has been surveyed. question: Do I need to notify this job?
reference_answer: I need to know the material, its condition, the method and how long the work will take. question: How long do I need to keep the asbestos paperwork?

question: What mask do the lads need for this?

question: Roughly how much does an asbestos refurbishment survey cost for a two-bed flat?

question: What does the local tip charge per tonne to take asbestos cement sheets, and do they need booking?

question: A retired bricklayer we used to employ has been diagnosed with mesothelioma. How does he claim compensation?

question: Can the housing association recharge leaseholders for the asbestos removal in the communal stairs through the service charge?

question: Customer wants their old combi swapped for a new one. My gas engineer is Gas Safe. Do I still have to tell building control or pay for an inspection?

The installer must, within 30 days of finishing, give the occupier a copy of the compliance certificate and give the building control authority notice or the certificate. The work must still meet the Building Regulations, for example the boiler efficiency rules in Approved Document L.

question: Bathroom refit, same layout, we're just ripping out the old suite and putting a new bath, toilet and basin back in the same spots. Is that notifiable?
reference_answer: Swapping a toilet (for one that uses no more water), a basin, a fixed bath or a shower is listed as work that needs no building notice or full plans, as long as there is no work to underground drainage and nothing done to the water supply or above-ground drainage that could harm anyone's health or safety. question: Homeowner wants a shower room put into a box bedroom upstairs where there's no plumbing at the moment. Do I need building regs sign-off, and can my plumber self-certify it?

question: What U-value do the new windows have to hit when we replace all the windows in a 1930s semi?
reference_answer: Replacement windows in an existing home should have a U-value of 1.4 W/m2K or better, or a Window Energy Rating of Band B or better, and be no worse than what they replace. Doors more than 60% glazed need 1.4 or Doorset Energy Rating Band C; other doors 1.4 or Band B. The units should also be draught-proofed, with insulated cavity closers where needed. question: The old windows we're taking out don't have trickle vents. Do the new ones need them?
reference_answer: Yes, usually. New windows make the house more airtight, so ventilation must be no worse than before. One way is background ventilators of at least 8000 mm2 equivalent area in habitable rooms and kitchens and 4000 mm2 in bathrooms. If the house has continuous mechanical extract, 4000 mm2 per habitable room is enough, and wet rooms can go without. If the old windows had trickle vents, the new ones must be no smaller and must be controllable.

question: Single storey rear extension, client wants a massive wall of bifolds and two roof lanterns. Is there a limit on how much glass I can put in?
reference_answer: Under the simple elemental route, total windows, roof windows, rooflights and doors in the extension should not be more than 25% of the extension floor area plus the area of any windows and doors that are lost or covered by the extension. question: What U-values does building control want for walls, roof and floor on a new extension?
reference_answer: New thermal elements in an extension should meet the limits for new elements in existing homes: roof 0.15, walls 0.18 and floor 0.18 W/m2K (area-weighted averages). A lesser wall standard may be accepted if it would cut a room's floor area by more than 5%, and the floor U-value can be worked out using the perimeter and area of the whole enlarged house. question: Loft conversion. Do we have to upgrade the existing roof slope and the gable walls that become part of the new room, or just insulate the new bits?
reference_answer: Existing elements kept in a loft or garage conversion should be upgraded if their U-value is worse than the threshold: roof worse than 0.35 should be improved to 0.16, and a wall worse than 0.70 to 0.30 with internal or external insulation. If that is not technically or functionally feasible, or would not pay back within 15 years, upgrade as far as is feasible within a 15-year payback; generally the result should not be worse than 0.7. A lesser roof standard may be fine where it would limit headroom.

question: We're hacking off all the old plaster on the back wall of a solid brick terrace and re-plastering. Someone said that triggers having to insulate it. True?
reference_answer: It can. Stripping an element back to the bricks and rebuilding, or dry-lining it, counts as renovating a thermal element. If more than 50% of that wall's surface is renovated (or it is a major renovation), the whole wall should be brought up to 0.30 W/m2K for internal insulation, as far as technically, functionally and economically feasible. A lesser standard may be acceptable if insulating would cut the room's floor area by more than 5% or would not pay back in 15 years. Renovation of thermal elements is notifiable work.

question: Replacing the felt on a flat roof garage extension with a new rubber membrane. Does that need building control, and do I have to add insulation?
reference_answer: Replacing the waterproof membrane on a flat roof counts as renovating a thermal element. If more than 50% of the roof is done, the whole roof should be upgraded towards 0.16 W/m2K where feasible (lesser standards are allowed for upstand height or structural limits). Replacing a roof covering is notifiable, but a roofer registered with NAPIT or the NFRC CompetentRoofer scheme can self-certify it instead of you giving a building notice. If the garage is unheated it may not be a thermal element at all.

question: Stair rules for a loft conversion: max riser, min going, max pitch?
reference_answer: For a private stair in a house, each rise should be between 150 and 220 mm and each going between 220 and 300 mm, with a maximum pitch of 42 degrees. Twice the rise plus the going should normally be between 550 and 700 mm, and every step in a flight should be the same. In existing buildings follow these figures unless space makes it impossible, and agree any alternative with building control.

question: Can't get 2 metres headroom over the new loft stairs because of the roof slope. What will building control accept?
reference_answer: The normal clear headroom over a stair is 2 m. In a loft conversion where there is not enough space for that, a reduced headroom is accepted: 1.9 m at the centre line of the stair, falling to 1.8 m at the side of the stair (measured at half the stair width).

question: Tiny landing, no room for a normal staircase into the loft. Client is asking about one of those paddle space-saver stairs or even a fixed ladder. Allowed?
reference_answer: An alternating tread (paddle) stair can be used only in a loft conversion, only where there is no room for a normal stair, and only to reach one habitable room plus, if wanted, a bathroom or WC that is not the only WC in the house. It needs handrails on both sides, slip-resistant treads, a maximum rise of 220 mm and minimum going of 220 mm (measured between alternate nosings), and 2 m clear headroom. A fixed ladder with handrails both sides is allowed only for a loft with one habitable room where a stair cannot fit. Retractable ladders must not be the escape route.

question: Fitting new spindles and handrail on a family house stair. How high does the handrail go and what gap between spindles?
reference_answer: The top of the handrail should be 900 to 1000 mm above the pitch line or floor, and stairs 1000 mm or wider need a handrail on both sides. Guarding on a house stair or landing should be at least 900 mm high. Where children under five may use the house, no gap should let a 100 mm sphere through and the guarding should be hard to climb.

question: Which glass needs to be toughened or laminated? Fitting a glazed back door with side panels and a low window next to it.
topic: glazing: safety glass in critical locations
reference_answer: Critical locations are glazing in doors and in side panels near doors between floor level and 1500 mm, and glazing in windows and walls between floor level and 800 mm. There the glass must break safely (for example Class 3 of BS EN 12600 or Class C of BS 6206), be robust, be in small panes, or be permanently protected. Door or side panel panes wider than 900 mm can use Class 2 / Class B.

question: Digging footings for an extension on clay with a couple of big trees in next door's garden. How deep do I need to go?
reference_answer: Strip foundations not on rock should be at least 0.45 m deep for frost. On shrinkable clay the minimum depth is 0.75 m on low shrinkage, 0.9 m on medium and 1.0 m on high shrinkage clay, and these depths may need to be greater where trees are nearby or to reach good ground. With big trees close by, you will likely need deeper footings or an engineered design.

question: Customer wants a kitchen extension right over the line of the public sewer at the back. Building notice ok, or do I need something else first?
reference_answer: Building over or within 3 m of a sewer on the sewer map is covered by requirement H4, and for that work you must make a full plans application, not a building notice. Consult the sewerage undertaker who owns a public sewer. Do not build over or within 3 m of a sewer deeper than 3 m or wider than 225 mm without their permission, keep the length under the building to 6 m unless they agree, and do not cover a manhole on a sewer serving more than one property unless other access is agreed.

question: How high above the garden level does the DPC need to be on a new extension wall?
reference_answer: In an external wall the damp-proof course should be at least 150 mm above the adjoining ground, unless another part of the building protects the wall, and it should join up with the floor damp-proof membrane. question: Just put a new gas boiler in the kitchen. Do I have to fit a CO alarm and where does it go?
reference_answer: Yes. When a new or replacement fixed gas appliance (other than one used only for cooking) is fitted in a home, a carbon monoxide alarm should go in the same room. It should meet BS EN 50291-1 and run on a battery that lasts the life of the alarm with an end-of-life warning, or be a hard-wired mains Type A alarm with a sensor failure warning (not plug-in). Place it on the ceiling at least 300 mm from walls, or high on a wall but not within 150 mm of the ceiling, and 1 to 3 m from the appliance.

question: Customer's moving their heating oil tank to the side of the house. How close can it be to the house and the fence?
reference_answer: For a domestic heating oil tank up to 3500 litres, no extra measures are needed if it is at least 1800 mm from the building and 760 mm from the boundary. Closer than 1800 mm to the building, either make the building wall within 1800 mm imperforate with 30 minutes fire resistance and protect the eaves, or build a fire wall. Closer than 760 mm to the boundary, provide a fire wall or a 30-minute boundary wall extending 300 mm above and beyond the tank. A hard base under the tank, such as concrete or paving slabs at least 42 mm thick reaching 300 mm past its edges, is one way to stop fires spreading and the area getting overgrown. An OFTEC or similar registered installer can self-certify the tank.

question: We're fitting a wood burner into an existing fireplace in a lounge. What do I need: who signs it off, alarm, any label?

question: Boiler swap only, keeping the old rads and pipes. Do I have to design the heating for 55 degrees flow now? And what efficiency does the new boiler need?
reference_answer: The rule to size the whole system for a maximum 55 C flow temperature applies when a wet system is newly installed or fully replaced, including the boiler, emitters and pipework, so a boiler-only swap does not trigger it. A gas boiler for wet heating in an existing home should be at least 92% efficient (ErP), with lower SEDBUK figures only in exceptional cases. The system should be sized from a heat loss calculation and not oversized, and a combi should modulate down to the home's typical heating load.

question: Kitchen refit, the sparky's adding a few sockets off the existing ring and a new radial for the oven. Which bits are notifiable?
reference_answer: Only three kinds of electrical work in a home are notifiable: a new circuit, replacing a consumer unit, and adding to or altering circuits in a special location (around a bath or shower, or a pool or sauna room). So the new oven radial is notifiable, and extra sockets off the existing ring in a kitchen are not. All the work must still be done to BS 7671 and meet Part P.

question: My electrician is qualified but not in NICEIC or NAPIT. He needs to change a consumer unit. How do we get it legal?
reference_answer: Replacing a consumer unit is notifiable. If the electrician is not a registered competent person, there are two routes. He can appoint a registered third-party certifier before starting; within 5 days of finishing he notifies them, they inspect and test, and their scheme sends the certificate to the occupier and building control within 30 days. Or he notifies building control before work begins, and they decide what inspection and testing they need (his own BS 7671 certificate can reduce this).

question: What counts as the 'special location' in a bathroom for electrics? How far from the shower?
reference_answer: In a room with a bath or shower, the special location is the space around the bath tap or shower head: up to 2.25 m above the finished floor (or up to the shower head if it is fixed higher), and out 0.6 m from the edge of the bath or shower tray. With no tray, it runs 1.2 m from the centre of the shower head. A room with a swimming pool or sauna heater also counts. New work or changes to circuits inside it are notifiable.

question: Building notice or full plans for a single storey extension? What's the real difference?
topic: procedure: building notice vs full plans
reference_answer: With full plans, the building control body checks drawings and gives a decision within 5 weeks (or 2 months if you agree), so you have formal approval before you build. A building notice is for smaller jobs: you can start 2 days after giving it, but there is no formal approval and the body can ask for plans later. You must use full plans if the building is covered by the Fire Safety Order, fronts a private street, or the work is over or near a mapped sewer. A building notice lapses after 3 years if work has not started.

question: Plans are passed. How much notice do I give building control before we dig, and what's this 'commencement' notice after we start?
topic: procedure: notices at start of work
reference_answer: You must not start until you have told the building control authority you intend to start and at least two days have passed after the day you gave that notice. Separately, within five days after the work counts as commenced, you must send a notice saying so. For a horizontal extension, work counts as commenced once the foundations and ground floor structure are complete. The authority can reject the notice within four weeks if it does not agree work has commenced. Building control can also ask you to notify them at stages they plan to inspect.
cited_clauses: br2010 regulation 16(1) (two days' notice before starting)

question: Bought a house to do up and the loft was converted by the last owner with no paperwork. Can we get it signed off now?
reference_answer: You can apply to the local authority (not a private approver) for a regularisation certificate, which is retrospective approval. It only covers work done on or after 11 November 1985. The council may ask you to open up work or test it, and tell you what extra work is needed; it has no duty to issue the certificate. The regularisation charge must be paid with the application or it is not valid.
cited_clauses: manual-br paragraphs B13 to B17 (regularisation certificates)

question: Big loft job: client hired their own architect, a separate steel fabricator and us as main builder, but never appointed anyone in writing as principal designer or contractor. Who is it by default?
topic: dutyholders: domestic client fails to appoint
reference_answer: If a domestic client does not make the appointments, the designer in control of the design phase is the principal designer and the contractor in control of the construction phase is the principal contractor. With more than one contractor, the client's duties pass to the principal contractor (or to the principal designer if they agree that in writing with the client).
cited_clauses: br2010 regulation 11C(2) (default principal designer and principal contractor)

question: What actually changes with the Future Homes Standard in 2026/27 for a firm like mine doing extensions, windows and boilers?
reference_answer: The amending regulations and the new Approved Documents L and F apply in England from 24 March 2027 (24 September 2027 for higher-risk buildings). Part L is renamed to cover greenhouse gas emissions, and new homes must have on-site renewable electricity, usually solar PV. For work on existing homes, the limiting U-values stay the same, for example windows 1.4 or Band B, walls 0.18 and roofs 0.15 for new elements. Work notified before 24 March 2027 can stay on the old rules only if it starts before 24 March 2028.

question: Put a building notice in February 2027 for an extension but the client wants to wait and start in spring 2028. Old Part L or new?
reference_answer: The old rules continue only where the building notice, initial notice or full plans was given before 24 March 2027 and the work starts before 24 March 2028. If you start on or after 24 March 2028, the 2026 amendments and new guidance apply. For an extension, work counts as started when the foundations and ground floor structure are complete, so starting to dig is not enough.

question: Does the new 2026 ventilation document change the fan size for a bathroom?
reference_answer: No. The 2026 Approved Document F Volume 1 still gives 15 l/s intermittent extract for a bathroom, the same as the 2021 edition. The 2026 edition takes effect on 24 March 2027 for work that is not higher-risk building work.
label_note: relabel: adf-2026 Table 1.1 (bathroom 15 l/s) and front matter (24 March 2027); adf Table 1.1

question: Client wants a downstairs toilet straight off the kitchen. Do I need a lobby between them?
reference_answer: A room with a toilet must be separated from a kitchen or food preparation area. In a home, a room with both a toilet and a basin only needs a door between it and the kitchen, not a separate lobby. If the toilet room has no basin, the hand washing space must be entered before the food area and separated from it by a door.

question: Loft conversion with a new bedroom and shower room. Does building control care about sound between the new rooms and the floor below?
topic: sound: loft conversion internal walls and floors
reference_answer: New internal floors, and internal walls between a bedroom or a room with a WC and other rooms, should give reasonable sound resistance: at least 40 dB Rw airborne (laboratory value) for walls and floors. This does not apply to internal walls that contain a door, or to a wall between an en-suite toilet and its bedroom.
cited_clauses: ade requirement E2 and its limits on application

question: Loft conversion in a terrace. We need to pocket the steel beam into the party wall. What notice do I give the neighbour and how long before?
topic: party wall: cutting in for a beam
reference_answer: Cutting into a party wall, for example to bear a beam, is work under section 2 of the Party Wall Act. Before doing it you must serve a party structure notice on the adjoining owner at least two months before the start date, giving your details, the work and the start date. If they do not consent within 14 days, a dispute is deemed to have arisen and surveyors are appointed. The notice lapses if work does not start within 12 months.
cited_clauses: party-wall-act-1996 section 2(2)(f) (cut into a party structure)
party-wall-act-1996 section 3(1) and (2) (party structure notice, two months)

question: Rear extension footings will be about 2 m from the neighbour's back wall and deeper than their foundations. Party wall notice needed even if I'm not touching their wall?
reference_answer: Yes. Digging within 3 m of a neighbour's building to below the bottom of their foundations needs a notice under section 6, served at least one month before you start, saying whether you plan to underpin or protect their foundations. Within 6 m the Act applies if the dig would cut a 45 degree line down from their foundations. If they do not consent within 14 days, a dispute is deemed to have arisen.
cited_clauses: party-wall-act-1996 section 6(5) and (7) (one month notice, 14 days)
label_note: 6(1) within 3 m and below their foundations; 6(2) within 6 m, 45 degree line; 6(5) one month notice; booklet para 28 (para 29 also says one month)

question: Served party wall notice three weeks ago, neighbour hasn't replied at all. Can I just crack on?
reference_answer: No. For work on an existing party wall or excavation, silence for 14 days means a dispute is deemed to have arisen. It then goes to surveyors: an agreed surveyor, or one each with a third surveyor, who make an award. If the neighbour will not appoint one, the building owner can appoint a surveyor on their behalf. You also cannot start before the notice period (one or two months) ends unless the neighbour agrees in writing.
label_note: Booklet 49: silence for 14 days means a dispute; s5 deemed dispute; s10(1) surveyors settle it (10(4) appointing on the neighbour's behalf)

question: Do I need a party wall notice just to chase in new sockets and re-plaster the party wall side of a lounge?
reference_answer: Probably not. The government booklet says drilling for shelves or units, cutting in recessed wiring and sockets, and replastering may be too minor to need a notice. The test is whether the work could affect the wall's strength and support or damage the neighbour's side; if in doubt, take advice from a building professional.
label_note: Booklet para 6: shelves, recessed wiring and sockets, replastering may be too minor for a notice

question: Semi-detached house, client wants a 5 metre single storey rear extension without full planning. Can we do it under permitted development?
reference_answer: For a house that is not detached, a single storey rear extension can go up to 3 m beyond the original rear wall under permitted development, with a maximum height of 4 m. Outside article 2(3) land and SSSIs, it can go up to 6 m, but only through the neighbour consultation (prior approval) scheme: you notify the council and cannot start until it says prior approval is not needed, grants it, or 42 days pass with no decision. Building regulations approval is still needed separately.

question: Rear dormer loft conversion on a mid-terrace. What are the permitted development limits?
reference_answer: On a terraced house the roof can grow by no more than 40 cubic metres over the original roof space (50 for other houses), counting any earlier roof extensions. A dormer is not allowed on a roof slope forming the principal elevation that fronts a highway, and not on article 2(3) land. Materials should look similar, the dormer should be set back about 0.2 m from the eaves where practicable, no balconies, and side-facing windows must be obscure glazed and fixed below 1.7 m from the floor.

question: Small conservatory at the back, about 12 square metres, on a dwarf wall. Building regs or exempt?
reference_answer: A ground-level conservatory or porch of no more than 30 m2 is exempt, as long as its glazing meets the safety glazing rules in Part K. It must keep thermal separation from the house (an external-quality wall and door). If that separation is removed or the house heating is extended into it, it is treated as an extension and the energy rules apply. Any electrics are still covered by Part P.
label_note: Sched 2 Class 7: ground-level conservatory up to 30 m2 exempt if glazing meets Part K (the 30 m2 and glazing condition are in wrapper3n2, the conservatory list in wrapper2n2); ADL 10.12 thermal separation; 9(3) Part P still applies

question: Garden office/summerhouse, about 20 square metres, timber, half a metre off the fence, with power run from the house. Does it need building regs?
reference_answer: A detached single storey building up to 15 m2 with no sleeping accommodation is exempt. Between 15 and 30 m2 it is exempt only if it is at least 1 m from the boundary or built substantially of non-combustible material, so a 20 m2 timber building 0.5 m from the fence would not be exempt. Either way, electrics fed from the house are still covered by Part P.

question: Customer wants cavity wall insulation blown in. Building control job or can the installer self-certify? And is the old UF foam stuff still allowed?
reference_answer: Putting insulation into a cavity wall is building work. An installer registered for it (for example with Blue Flame, CERTASS, the Insulation Assurance Authority, Certsure or NAPIT) can self-certify; otherwise notify building control. Urea formaldehyde foam can still be used only where the inner leaf is masonry, the wall is assessed first to BS 8208-1, the installer holds a current registration of assessed capability, and the material follows BS 5617 and BS 5618.
cited_clauses: br2010 regulation 3(1)(e) (cavity insulation is building work)

question: Taking out a chimney breast in a back bedroom on a terrace. Building control? Neighbour?
reference_answer: Removing a chimney breast is listed as work that may need building regulations approval, because it affects the structure. If the breast is on a party wall, cutting it away is work under section 2 of the Party Wall Act, so you need to serve a party structure notice at least two months before. The Act is separate from building regulations, so you need both.

question: Customer's asking for the boiler compliance certificate. How long has the installer got to send it?
reference_answer: The Building Regulations say a self-certifying installer must give the occupier a copy of the certificate, and give the building control authority notice or the certificate, within 30 days of finishing. The Manual to the Building Regulations says to contact the scheme operator if it has not arrived within 30 days. Note that the current GOV.UK approval page says the certificate comes within 8 weeks, so the sources do not quite agree; the regulation (30 days) is the legal rule.
cited_clauses: br-approval Use a competent person scheme (within 8 weeks)

question: Can I use reclaimed bricks from the demo on the new extension walls, or does building control want new stamped stuff?
reference_answer: Building work must use adequate and proper materials, but they do not have to be new. Past experience, such as successful use in an existing building, can show a material is fit for its purpose; tests, calculations or certification are other ways. The local authority can take samples to check materials comply.
label_note: 1.18 past experience such as use in an existing building; reg 7(1) adequate and proper materials; 1.17 tests and calculations; 1.19 sampling

question: Is it the council or can I use a private inspector? And can I switch to a private one halfway through after we've already started without telling anyone?
topic: procedure: choosing a building control body
reference_answer: For work that is not on a higher-risk building, you can use your local authority or a registered building control approver; if you use an approver, they give the local authority an initial notice. If work has already started or finished without notifying anyone, you cannot use a private approver: only the local authority can deal with it, through regularisation, and it is not obliged to approve it.
cited_clauses: manual-br Volume 1 Chapter 4 Using a building control body
label_note: relabel: manual-br Vol 1 chapter 4 (using a building control body, regularisation) and Vol 2 chapter B (B4); GOV.UK where to apply

question: Bathroom refit in a normal house, new bath going in. Do regs make me fit a TMV to stop the bath going over 48 degrees?
reference_answer: Not for a refit of an existing home. The 48 C limit on hot water to a fixed bath applies only when a dwelling is newly built or formed by a material change of use (for example a new flat in a converted building). Where it applies, an in-line blending valve or similar with a maximum temperature stop is the usual way to meet it.
cited_clauses: adg requirement G3(4) and its limits on application
label_note: relabel: ADG G3 requirement box with limits on application; 3.65 blending valve 48 C; Sched 1 G3 kept

question: Client says the new rear extension has to have a level threshold and wheelchair-width doors because of Part M. Is that right?
reference_answer: No. Requirement M4(1) and the guidance in Approved Document M Volume 1 apply to new dwellings and to dwellings undergoing material alteration, not to the extension of a dwelling. Where a material alteration is made, the house should be no less compliant with M4(1) than before the work. The client may still want those features, but the regulations do not require them for an extension.
cited_clauses: adm requirement M4(1) limits on application
label_note: relabel: ADM Vol 1 0.2 (not extensions), M4(1) with limits on application, 0.11 material alterations; Sched 1 M4(1) kept

question: Replacing windows on an old house. Do they all have to be PAS 24 security rated now because of Part Q?
reference_answer: No. Requirement Q1 (resisting unauthorised access) applies only to new dwellings, including those formed by a material change of use. It does not apply to replacement windows in an existing house, although secure windows are still a good idea. Replacement windows must meet the energy and ventilation rules.
cited_clauses: adq requirement Q1 limits on application (new dwellings only)
label_note: relabel: ADQ 0.2 (new dwellings only), Q1 text with limits on application; Sched 1 Q1 kept

question: Since Part T came in, does a new downstairs loo in a house have to be a universal toilet?
reference_answer: No. Requirement T1 covers toilet accommodation in buildings other than dwellings, such as shops or offices. A toilet in a house is covered by Part G (at least one WC and hand basin, separated from the kitchen) and, for new houses, Part M.
cited_clauses: adt requirement T1 (buildings other than dwellings)
label_note: relabel: T1 is toilet accommodation in buildings other than dwellings (ADT T1, 1.1); G4 and ADG 4.8 cover dwellings

question: We've got planning and building regs approved for the loft, so the party wall stuff is covered too, yeah?
reference_answer: No. The Party Wall Act is separate from planning permission and building regulations. Having those approvals does not remove the need to serve notices under the Act where the work is covered, such as cutting into a party wall for a beam. The council has no duty to tell you about the Act. If you start without notice, the neighbour can seek a court injunction.
label_note: Booklet 57: the Act is separate from planning and building regs; 58: council has no duty to tell; 48: what happens if no notice; guidance intro says the same

question: Do I now have to put an EV charger in when I build a house extension with a driveway?
reference_answer: No. Part S applies to new residential buildings, buildings that undergo a material change of use into dwellings, and major renovations where the building will have more than 10 associated parking spaces. A house extension is not one of these, so no charge point is required.
cited_clauses: ads paragraph 0.3 (types of building work covered)
ads requirement S3 and paragraph 2.10 (major renovation, more than 10 spaces)

question: Combustible cladding ban: does that mean I can't put timber cladding on a two storey house extension?
reference_answer: No. The ban in regulation 7(2) applies only to relevant buildings, which have a storey at least 18 m above ground and contain dwellings, an institution or residential rooms. A two-storey house is far below that. The external wall must still meet the general fire safety requirements of Part B.
label_note: 7(4) relevant building has a storey at least 18 m high; 7(2) the ban; bamd2018 reg 2(7) inserted it

question: Building control will want an overheating assessment for our loft conversion with big rooflights, under Part O?
reference_answer: No. Approved Document O applies only to new residential buildings (new dwellings, care homes, student rooms and similar). A loft conversion in an existing house is not covered by Part O. The extra glazing is still limited by the energy rules in Part L.
label_note: relabel: ADO 0.3 (new residential buildings only); O1; ADL 10.5 limits glazing

question: Got a job in Glasgow, side extension on a bungalow. What's the process for a building warrant up there?
reference_answer: Not covered. These documents cover the Building Regulations for England; the GOV.UK page only notes that Scotland has different rules. You would need the Scottish building standards and the local council's building warrant guidance.

question: There's an oak with a tree preservation order right where the extension footings go. Do I need council consent to cut the roots?
reference_answer: Not covered. The documents deal with foundation depth near trees on clay, but not with tree preservation order consent. You would need the planning rules on protected trees and to ask the local planning authority.
label_note: Out of scope: no parsed section answers it

question: What size steel do I need over a 4.5 metre opening where we're knocking the kitchen and dining room through?
reference_answer: Not covered. The documents say removing a load-bearing wall may need building regulations approval, but they do not give steel beam sizes. You need a structural engineer's calculation for the actual loads, which building control will check.

question: What cable size and RCD rating do I need for a 10.5 kW electric shower?
reference_answer: Not covered. Approved Document P says electrical work should follow BS 7671 and a new shower circuit is notifiable, but cable sizes and protective device ratings are in BS 7671 itself, which is not in these documents. An electrician needs to design the circuit to BS 7671.

question: How much will my local council charge for a building notice on a 25 square metre extension?
reference_answer: Not covered. The rules say each local authority sets its own charging scheme based on its costs and publishes it, but they do not give amounts. You need the charging scheme on that council's website, or a quote from a registered building control approver.
label_note: Out of scope: no parsed section answers it

question: Found Japanese knotweed at the bottom of the garden where the extension is going. What are the rules for getting rid of it?
reference_answer: Not covered. The site preparation guidance deals with contaminants and moisture, not invasive plants or their disposal. You would need environmental and waste guidance and a specialist contractor.

question: How long does the council take to decide a normal householder planning application for a two storey extension?
reference_answer: Not covered. The permitted development guide gives the 42-day period for prior approval of larger single storey extensions, but not the time limits for a full householder planning application. You would need planning procedure guidance or the local planning authority.

question: Do I need building control for this job?
reference_answer: It depends on the work. Building regulations cover new buildings, extensions, material alterations, new or changed controlled services and fittings (such as boilers, windows and bathrooms), changes of use, cavity insulation and underpinning. Some small jobs are exempt or listed as not needing notice, and work by a registered competent person needs no application. Tell me what you are doing, where, and who is doing each part.

question: What U-value do I need to hit?
reference_answer: That depends on the element (wall, roof, floor, window, door) and the job: a new house, an extension or new element in an existing home, or renovating or keeping an existing element. For example, new walls in an extension are 0.18, a renovated wall with internal insulation 0.30, and replacement windows 1.4. Tell me the element and the type of work.

question: Is my staircase going to pass?
reference_answer: I need the rise and going of each step, the pitch, the headroom, the handrail and guarding details, and whether it is a new house stair or a loft conversion. For a house stair, rises are 150 to 220 mm, goings 220 to 300 mm, maximum pitch 42 degrees, and headroom 2 m (reduced in lofts).

question: Do I need to serve a party wall notice?
reference_answer: It depends on what you are doing and where. The Act covers building a new wall on the boundary (one month's notice), work to an existing party wall such as cutting in or raising it (two months), and digging within 3 m or 6 m of a neighbour's building below their foundation level (one month). Tell me the work, how close it is to next door, and how deep you dig.

question: What size extractor fan does building control want?
reference_answer: That depends on the room and the type of system. Intermittent rates are 15 l/s for a bathroom, 6 l/s for a toilet, 30 l/s for a utility room, and 30 or 60 l/s for a kitchen depending on whether a cooker hood vents outside. Continuous systems have different rates. Which room is it, and is the fan intermittent or continuous?

question: We're swapping the flat front doors in a council block. What fire rating do the new doorsets need, and do they all need closers?
reference_answer: A flat front door in the wall between a flat and a shared corridor or lobby should be a 30-minute doorset with smoke control: E 30 Sa on the European test, or FD 30S on the BS 476-22 test. Every fire doorset, flat front doors included, should have a self-closing device. From 2 September 2029 the BS 476 route is removed from AD B and only the European classification (30 minutes, Sa) is listed.
cited_clauses: adb-amendments 2029 booklet Appendix C Table C1

question: Who's meant to check the fire doors in our 14-storey council block, and how often?
reference_answer: The responsible person (for council blocks, normally the council as landlord) has the duty. In a building with two or more flats whose top storey is over 11m, flat front doors must be checked at least once every 12 months on a best-endeavours basis, and fire doors in the shared areas at least once every 3 months. Both checks must cover whether the self-closers work. Records must be kept, including what was tried when a resident would not let you in.
label_note: reg 10(4) annual flat doors, 10(6) 3-monthly communal, 10(7) closers, 10(5) records; guide 6.1 restates

question: Tenant on the 6th floor keeps refusing to let us in to check her front door closer. Is the council in breach?
reference_answer: The annual flat door check is a best-endeavours duty, so not getting in is not automatically a breach, but the responsible person must record each step taken to try to get access in every 12-month period. Guidance suggests booking visits in advance and offering a choice of times, keeping letters and emails as evidence, and in the end legal action may be considered if a resident keeps refusing.
cited_clauses: fser-page Fact sheet: Fire doors (regulation 10), Problems with access
label_note: best endeavours in 10(4), record of steps in 10(5); guide 6.5-6.6 on booking access and evidence

question: When we check fire doors, what's the biggest gap round the door that's acceptable?
reference_answer: The government fire door guidance quotes the industry standard of no more than 4mm between door and frame. At the bottom the gap should be kept as small as you can while making sure the door will not catch on the floor if it drops a little on its hinges. Cheap gap-tester cards can be used for the check.
label_note: 6.7(g): 4mm industry standard, bottom gap as small as practicable

question: What's the proper way to test a closer on a fire door so I know it's actually working?
reference_answer: Open the door all the way and let go, then open it only about 15 degrees and let go again. Both times it must shut fully into the frame on its own, beating the latch and any rubbing on the floor. The regulations require the routine fire door checks to include making sure self-closers work.
label_note: 6.7(h): open fully then about 15 degrees; reg 10(7) checks include closers

question: Corridor doors are held open on magnets wired to the fire alarm. How do we test the closers without wrecking the hold-opens?
reference_answer: Release the door with the test button where there is one, not by pulling it off the magnet. AD B lets a fire door with a closer be held open if an automatic release, triggered by the building's fire alarm and detection, lets it shut, so smoke detectors must be present. The weekly alarm test is also the time to check that these releases let the doors go.

question: Riser cupboard doors on each landing, do they need closers fitted and how often should someone look at them?
reference_answer: In blocks over 11m, riser, plant room and service cupboard doors get the same 3-monthly check as other communal fire doors. They may either self-close or be kept locked. AD B does not ask for closers on service duct doors that are normally locked, but these should carry the BS 5499-5 'keep locked shut' fire door sign. In a protected shaft wall the door should be rated at half the wall's period, at least 30 minutes.
label_note: 6.12 three-monthly, 6.13 self-closing or locked; C5(b) no closer on locked service duct doors; C11(b) keep locked shut sign

question: A leaseholder on the 3rd floor has put in a composite front door without asking anyone. No idea if it's fire rated. What happens now?
reference_answer: In a block with two or more flats the Fire Safety Order covers every flat-to-corridor door, so the responsible person has to deal with it. Where it is unclear, the resident must show the new door resists fire, was fitted by someone competent, and hand over its technical details; front door changes should only happen if the responsible person agrees. The LGA guide treats a front door that neither resists fire nor self-closes as a significant risk, and the usual fix is an FD30S door with a positive-action closer.

question: Original 1970s flat doors, no intumescent strips, FRA calls them 'notional FD30'. What can we offer the council apart from ripping them all out?
reference_answer: The guide gives three choices: keep the door if it fits its frame well and met the fire door standard of its day; upgrade it by adding intumescent strips, smoke seals and a fire-protected letterbox, which only makes sense on a solid door of enough thickness (around 44mm); or replace it with a certified FD30S door. Whichever is chosen, flat front doors and doors protecting corridors and stairs need a positive-action self-closer; rising butt hinges are no longer seen as good enough.

question: The Fire Safety England Regs mean every flat front door now has to meet today's certified standard, so we should quote to replace the lot, yeah?
reference_answer: No. The revised government guidance says the regulations are not there to bring existing doors up to the standard for new blocks. A door that met the standard of its day will usually still do its job if it is undamaged and the gaps are not too big; missing strips, seals or certificates do not by themselves make it unfit. Whether a door is good enough is a question for the fire risk assessment under the Order, and nothing requires a door to be replaced just because it falls short of current Building Regulations.

question: Do the 3-monthly fire door checks have to be done by a third-party certified fire door inspector?
topic: who can do fire door checks
reference_answer: No. The regulation 10 checks are meant to be simple and visual, with no tools, and caretakers, housing officers, managing agents or maintenance staff can do them once shown how. Any repair or replacement the checks show up must be carried out promptly by a competent firm. The checks do not replace the periodic look at doors by fire specialists that forms part of the fire risk assessment.
cited_clauses: fser-fire-doors closing note on specialist assessment
label_note: 6.3 simple visual checks, no specialist; 6.4 repairs by competent contractor; 6.14 not a substitute for periodic specialist assessment

question: Our block's only 4 storeys, top floor about 9m up. We need to start doing the quarterly door checks as well, right?
reference_answer: Not under the regulations: the annual flat door checks and the 3-monthly communal door checks only apply where the top storey is above 11m. But the duty to give residents fire door information applies to every block with two or more flats and shared escape routes, whatever the height. Below 11m the responsible person must still keep all fire doors, flat front doors included, good enough under the general duties in the Order.
