question: Inside the flat, the doors off the hallway, what rating do they need and do they want closers on?
reference_answer: Doors that are part of the protected hallway or landing inside a flat should give 20 minutes' fire resistance. AD B does not ask for self-closers on fire doors inside flats. The AD B FAQ confirms closers are not needed on these internal doors even where they give lobby protection to a common stair, but the fire doors themselves are still recommended and residents should be told to keep them shut, especially at night.
label_note: Table C1 item 9: 20 min within flats; C5(c) no closers within flats; FAQ 5 confirms

question: What does the council legally have to tell residents about fire doors?
reference_answer: In any building with two or more flats and common parts used for escape, residents must be told to keep fire doors closed when not in use, that they and visitors must not interfere with self-closers, and to report any door fault or damage to the responsible person straight away. New residents must get this promptly after moving in, and all residents must be reminded at least once a year.
label_note: reg 10(1)-(3) required information and when; guide 5.2-5.3 restate

question: Are flat front doors the council's job under fire safety law, or are they the tenant's own business?
reference_answer: The Fire Safety Act 2021 changed the Order so that, in any building with two or more flats, it covers the structure, the external walls, the common parts and all doors between flats and the common parts. So flat front doors fall within the council's fire risk assessment. The fire door guidance says whoever is responsible for the communal parts carries out the regulation 10 checks, and that flat front doors count as common parts for that purpose.
label_note: art 6(1A)(b) all doors between flats and common parts (inserted by FSA 2021 s1); 6(1A) and 6(1B) sit inside article-6

question: We're running new pipes through the compartment wall between a flat and the corridor. What fire stopping do I need?
reference_answer: A pipe through a fire-separating wall or floor (other than inside a protected shaft) should use one of three methods: a proprietary tested seal for any pipe size; fire-stopping around the pipe with the hole kept as tight as possible and the pipe within the Table 9.1 size limits; or, for lead, aluminium, fibre-cement or uPVC pipes up to 160mm, a sleeve of metal that will not melt in a fire, as in Diagram 9.2. Service holes should be few, as small as practicable, and fire-stopped in a way that lets the pipe move with heat.
label_note: 9.2 three methods: 9.3 proprietary seal, 9.4 fire-stopping within Table 9.1 sizes, 9.5 sleeving

question: 110mm plastic soil stack through the floor between two flats. Can I just fire-stop round it?
reference_answer: Only if it fits the Table 9.1 rules. For a compartment floor between flats, a uPVC stack (to BS 4514 or 5255) can be up to 160mm (branches 110mm) with simple fire-stopping, but only when it is drainage boxed in the way Diagram 9.1 shows, with a casing of at least E 30 that is not sheet metal. If it is not enclosed that way, the 40mm limit for 'any other situation' applies, so a 110mm pipe would need a proprietary tested seal or the sleeve method.
label_note: Table 9.1 situation 2 uPVC stack 160mm in an enclosure per Diagram 9.1; 9.4 fire-stopping route

question: 22mm copper heating pipe going through a compartment wall, what do I have to do?
reference_answer: Copper is treated as a metal that will not melt or split in a fire, and Table 9.1 allows such pipes up to 160mm nominal bore in any situation without a proprietary seal. Keep the hole tight and fire-stop the gap around the pipe, allowing for the pipe's thermal movement.
label_note: Table 9.1 column (a) high melting point metal up to 160mm; 9.4 tight opening, fire-stop; 9.24(b) thermal movement

question: There's a big hole round a bunch of cables in a riser wall. Can I just pack it with mineral wool?
reference_answer: Openings for cables should be as few and as small as practicable and fire-stopped. Where the fire-stopping spans more than 100mm unsupported, or a non-rigid material is used without suitable fire test evidence, it should be reinforced or supported by class A2-s3, d2 (or better) material so it cannot be pushed out. Mineral fibre and rock-based products are listed as possible fire-stopping materials, but not every material suits every situation, and proprietary tested systems are available.
label_note: 9.25 reinforce or support over 100mm unsupported or non-rigid without test evidence; 9.24 openings few and small; 9.26-9.27 materials

question: What fire rating does the wall between a flat and the common corridor need?
reference_answer: Treat the corridor as a protected route; each flat's wall onto it is a compartment wall. It needs REI 30 if the top floor of the block is no more than 5m above ground, and REI 60 in anything taller. Walls that cut a flat off from any other part of the block are compartment walls too.
label_note: 3.38 REI 30 up to 5m else REI 60; 7.1(b) walls separating a flat are compartment walls

question: Gas riser running up the stairwell of a block. Is that allowed?
topic: gas pipes in protected stairs and shafts
reference_answer: Gas pipes and meters should be kept out of a protected stairway unless they are installed to the 1996 pipelines safety rules and the 1998 gas installation and use rules. In a protected shaft, natural gas or LPG pipes should be screwed or all-welded steel, installed to those same rules, and a shaft carrying piped gas needs vents to open air at both the top and the bottom.
label_note: 3.83 gas pipes not in protected stairway unless to 1996/1998 regs; 7.27-7.28 gas pipes and ventilation in protected shafts

question: Retrofitting fire collars on plastic waste pipes in occupied flats is a nightmare. What's actually expected in an existing block?
topic: fire stopping in existing occupied blocks
reference_answer: The LGA guide says small pipes, below about 40mm, are not normally a concern, but larger ones, especially combustible ones, can leave an opening in a fire. Proprietary seals or collars, or fire-resisting boxing, can be used in older blocks, but because of the difficulty in occupied flats it may only be practicable over time as flats become empty. Checking fire stopping inside flats usually needs opening up, which only happens in the destructive (Type 2 or 4) fire risk assessments.

question: We're starting a kitchen and bathroom programme in occupied council flats. What fire precautions will the council expect from us on site?
topic: fire safety during works in occupied blocks
reference_answer: The LGA guide says building work is the main hazardous activity in blocks of flats. Landlords should write fire precautions into contracts, check method statements and inspect while work is going on, small jobs included. Hot work should be controlled by a permit to work, with checks of the area before and after and extinguishers to hand. Typical problems to avoid are holes left through compartment walls or floors, stair doors removed or propped, blocked fire main inlets, gas bottles left inside overnight, combustible materials stored in common parts and opened-up structure without fire-resisting hoarding.

question: As the council's repairs contractor, do we carry any legal duties under the Fire Safety Order, or is it all on the council?
reference_answer: The council is the responsible person, but the Order also puts its duties on anyone else with any control over the premises, as far as the matters under their control go. Someone who has a contract obligation to maintain or repair the premises, or for their safety, is treated as having control to the extent of that obligation. So a repairs contractor can share the duties for the work it is responsible for.
label_note: 5(4) contract to maintain or repair counts as control; 5(3) duties extend to persons with control; art 3 responsible person

question: Council tenant's flat, what smoke alarms does the landlord legally have to have in there?
reference_answer: Since 1 October 2022 social landlords are covered as well as private ones. The landlord must make sure every storey with a room people live in has a smoke alarm, check the alarms work on the day a new tenancy starts, and repair or replace an alarm after the tenant reports it faulty. The rules do not set the alarm type; guidance recommends alarms to BS 5839-6, sealed-for-life batteries if battery powered, normally fixed on the ceiling in a hall or landing.

question: Fitting a new combi boiler in a rented flat. Does the room need a CO alarm, and where do I put it?
reference_answer: Yes. Since the 2022 amendment a CO alarm is needed in any living room, bedroom, kitchen or similar room that has a fixed fuel-burning appliance, except where the only appliance is a gas cooker, so gas boilers are covered, not just solid fuel. The regulations do not say where it goes; guidance says follow the maker's instructions, generally at head height about 1 to 3 metres from the appliance, using alarms to BS 50291.

scoar-guidance What type of carbon monoxide alarm is required?
label_note: 4(1)(a)(ii) CO alarm in a room with a fixed combustion appliance other than a gas cooker; guidance on placement

question: There's a gas hob in the kitchen so the landlord has to put a CO alarm in there, right?
reference_answer: No. Gas cookers are specifically left out of the CO alarm duty. A CO alarm is needed in a living room, kitchen or other living space only if it has some other fixed combustion appliance, such as a gas boiler or a wood burner.
cited_clauses: scoar-guidance Where do carbon monoxide alarms need to be located?
label_note: 4(1)(a)(ii) excludes gas cookers

question: Tenant rang saying her smoke alarm keeps chirping. What does the council actually have to do?
reference_answer: Guidance says tenants should first try new batteries, and report to the landlord if it still does not work or they cannot change the batteries. Once a fault is reported, the landlord must promptly check whether the alarm works and repair or replace it if not. This duty covers reports made from 1 October 2022.
cited_clauses: scoar-guidance Does replacing a battery count as a repair?
label_note: 4(1)(c) repair or replace after a report; 4(3A) as soon as reasonably practicable; guidance on batteries

question: The council's a social landlord, so the smoke and CO alarm rules don't apply to their flats anyway?
reference_answer: Wrong since 1 October 2022. The amendment made any immediate landlord of a covered tenancy a 'relevant landlord', and the guidance says the rules apply to social as well as private rented homes. A council cannot enforce the rules on its own homes, but it is still bound by them, answers to the social housing regulator and can face judicial review.

scoar-guidance What if my landlord is a local authority?

question: Same block, but one flat's a leaseholder who bought from the council. Do the alarm regs cover his flat?
reference_answer: No. Long leases, and tenancies granting occupation for 7 years or more, are excluded tenancies, and the regulations do not cover owner-occupiers or shared-ownership homes. The landlord duties only apply to covered rented tenancies.
cited_clauses: scoar-guidance Which tenancies are exempt from these regulations?
scoar-guidance Do the regulations apply to owner occupiers?
label_note: Schedule para 2: long leases and 7 years+ excluded; guidance on owner occupiers

question: Refurbishing flats with building control involved. What standard of smoke alarms goes in each flat, and do we need a communal alarm system?
topic: alarms in flats under AD B
reference_answer: Each flat should have at least a Grade D2 Category LD3 system to BS 5839-6, with mains-powered smoke alarms to BS EN 14604 (heat alarms to BS 5446-2) and a backup power source such as a battery. Where compartmentation is good, a block normally does without a communal fire alarm. Detectors in the shared areas may be needed to trigger smoke control but usually do not sound an alarm.
label_note: 1.10 each flat per 1.1-1.4, communal alarm not normally needed; 1.1 Grade D2 LD3; 1.2 mains BS EN 14604; 1.4 standby supply

question: How often should the communal fire alarm in a block be tested and serviced?
reference_answer: The LGA guide recommends a simple test once a week by setting off a call point, which housing or maintenance staff can do; it should also check any linked actions such as door hold-open releases. The system should be serviced by a competent firm at least twice a year, with BS 5839-1 as the reference.

question: AOVs in the lobbies and emergency lights on the stairs, how often should they be tested?
reference_answer: Automatic or electrically operated smoke vents should be tried once a month using the manual controls, and their smoke detectors and controls tested at least yearly. Emergency lights that are not self-testing need a short functional test every month and a full-duration battery test every year, taking care the building is never left without escape lighting while the batteries charge back up.

question: In our 20-storey block, what has to be checked every month, and what if the firefighting lift goes down?
reference_answer: In a residential block of 18m or 7 storeys and up, the responsible person must check every month the firefighting lifts, any evacuation lifts and the essential firefighting kit: rising main inlets and outlets, smoke control, suppression, common-area detection and alarms, evacuation alert systems and alarm-linked door releases. Faults must be put right; if one is still not fixed after 24 hours, the local fire service must be told electronically as soon as practicable, and told again once it is fixed. Records of the checks must be available to residents.
cited_clauses: fser-page Fact sheet: Lifts and essential fire-fighting equipment (regulation 7)
label_note: reg 7 monthly checks of lifts and equipment, fault reporting to FRS; 6(7) key equipment; reg 3 18m or 7 storeys

question: Does the block need one of those secure information boxes for the fire brigade, and what's supposed to go in it?
reference_answer: Under the 2022 regulations the responsible person for a residential block of at least 18m or 7 storeys must fit and maintain one, holding the responsible person's name, address and UK phone number, details of others with access, and paper copies of the floor and building plans; the box must be inspected at least yearly. For new building work, AD B recommends a box in any block of flats whose top storey is over 11m. So the thresholds differ.
label_note: reg 4 secure information box and contents; reg 3 high-rise; 6(5) plans in the box; AD B 15.19 for new blocks over 11m

question: Sprinklers, at what height does a block of flats need them, and do they go in the corridors and stairs too?
reference_answer: AD B recommends sprinklers throughout any block of flats whose top storey is over 11m above ground, designed to BS 9251 for residential buildings. They go inside the flats; shared stairs, corridors and landings do not need them when those areas are kept fire sterile. The threshold was cut from 30m to 11m by the amendments that applied from 26 November 2020.
cited_clauses: br-circulars Circular letter on Approved Document B volume 1 and 2 (26 May 2020), Sprinklers
label_note: 7.4 sprinklers over 11m, in flats, not in fire-sterile common areas; E3 BS 9251; 2020 change summary (May 2020 booklet merged into adb)

question: Could we leave out sprinklers on our 13m block of new flats if we bump the walls between flats up to 2 hours?
reference_answer: That is not what the guidance supports. AD B recommends sprinklers in any block of flats whose top storey is over 11m. The AD B FAQ says making the walls between flats more fire resistant than AD B asks is unlikely to help occupants much and does nothing for whoever is in the flat that is on fire, while research shows sprinklers greatly cut deaths and injuries.
label_note: FAQ 13: higher wall rating gives no significant benefit; 7.4 sprinklers over 11m

question: We're adding a storey to a 10m block, which takes it over 11m. Does the sprinkler system go through all the flats or only on the top floor we're building?
reference_answer: Each case is judged on its merits. New flats created above the 11m trigger should get the same protection as a new building, so in most cases they will need sprinklers. Extra protection may also be needed in the existing part so the extension complies, and overall fire safety must not be made worse; the fire risk assessment may also call for more work.
cited_clauses: br-circulars Circular letter on Approved Document B volume 1 and 2 (26 May 2020), Extensions

question: What's this new second staircase rule, and does it catch jobs that were already in for approval?
reference_answer: From 30 September 2026, AD B says flats need at least two common stairs where the highest storey is 18m or more up (or where one escape route alone is not acceptable). The old guidance still applies if the building notice, initial notice or full plans were lodged ahead of 30 September 2026 and the work was sufficiently progressed before that date or within 18 months after it; for work on an existing building, 'sufficiently progressed' just means the work has started. Circular 01/2024 announced this and was later withdrawn and reissued as Circular 04/2024.
cited_clauses: circ-adb-2024 Consequential amendment and summary of transitional arrangements

question: What actually changed in AD B in 2025 and 2026, and what's the 2029 one about?
reference_answer: 2025 (from 2 March 2025): updated guidance on the fire safety information handed over under regulation 38, dropping the old BS 476 reaction-to-fire and roof classes, and sprinklers in every new care home. 2026 (from 30 September 2026): at least two common stairs in any block of flats that has a storey at 18m or more, design for evacuation lifts, a restructured Section 3 and new terms such as evacuation shaft and storey exit. 2029 (from 2 September 2029): the BS 476 fire resistance classes go, leaving only European classes. The transitional periods are 6, 18 and 6 months.

question: Overcladding a 12m council block. What class of insulation are we allowed to use?
reference_answer: Where a residential building has any storey at 11m or more, insulation and fillers in its outside walls should reach class A2-s1, d0 or better (masonry cavity walls built to Diagram 8.2 are an exception). If the block had a storey at 18m or more, regulation 7(2) would apply instead and every material in the wall must reach class A2-s1, d0 or A1, apart from the listed exemptions.
label_note: 10.7 A2-s1, d0 at 11m+ residential, masonry cavity exception; 10.6 and 10.14 reg 7(2) at 18m

question: Block's 8 storeys but only about 17m to the top floor. Is it higher-risk or not?
reference_answer: Yes, if it has two or more homes in it: a building is higher-risk if it is 18m or taller or has 7 or more storeys, so 8 storeys is enough on its own. Height is taken from ground level up to the top floor's floor surface, and when counting storeys you leave out any below ground and any that are only roof-top plant.
label_note: s65(1) 18m or 7 storeys and 2+ units; reg 5 height to top floor surface; reg 6(1) storeys to ignore

question: Block has a basement car park, 6 floors of flats above it and a roof garden on top. Is that 7 storeys?
reference_answer: No, it counts as 6. Storeys below ground are ignored, and a storey is below ground if any part of its ceiling is below the adjacent ground. Government guidance treats an open roof garden as not being a storey, and it is not used for height either; the department is consulting on putting this in the regulations. You would then still check whether the top floor is 18m or more up.
cited_clauses: hrb-existing introductory statement on roof gardens
label_note: 6(1)(a) ignore below-ground storeys, 6(3) ceiling test; guidance on open rooftops and the roof-garden statement

question: Two 8-storey council towers joined by a shared underground car park. Is that one higher-risk building or two?
reference_answer: Attached structures count as one building unless they contain independent sections. A section is its own building if it has an entrance and exit reachable from anywhere in it and either no access to other sections, or access only to sections with no homes in them. The guidance example of two towers sharing a party wall and an underground car park treats each tower as a separate building. Doors used only in emergencies or for maintenance do not count as access.

question: Fire stopping and communal door upgrades across a registered high-rise as part of a remediation job. Do we need BSR sign-off first, and how long does it take?
topic: building control approval for work to existing HRB
reference_answer: Yes. Work to an existing higher-risk building needs building control approval from the Building Safety Regulator before it starts, unless it is only exempt work, work done under a competent person scheme, or emergency repairs. Work affecting passive fire measures or the common parts is category A, so the application needs extra documents such as a competence declaration, construction and change control plans, a mandatory occurrence reporting plan, a compliance statement and a fire and emergency file. The regulator should decide within 8 weeks unless a longer period is agreed in writing.

question: Water leak has wrecked the fire stopping in a riser in a higher-risk block and it needs sorting today. Do we have to wait for BSR?
reference_answer: Urgent repairs needed because of a risk to people's health, safety or welfare can go ahead without prior approval where getting it first is not practicable. The client must tell the regulator what the work is and why it was urgent (BSR guidance says by close of the next working day after starting), send a copy to the Fire Safety Order responsible person, and afterwards apply to have the work regularised. Emergency repair status is not for problems caused by poor planning.

question: The fire service has served an enforcement notice on the tower, so that counts as emergency repairs and we can skip BSR approval, yes?
reference_answer: Not usually. BSR guidance says work needed to meet a fire service enforcement notice will rarely count as an emergency repair, because it is not work that must start straight away. Approval from the regulator may well be needed, and should speak to the fire service that served the notice about approval timescales.

question: Residents in the tower keep wedging the stair doors open and pulling smoke detectors off the ceiling. Is there any law aimed at the residents themselves?
reference_answer: Yes. In an occupied higher-risk building, residents aged 16 and over and flat owners must not do anything that creates a significant building safety risk and must not interfere with safety items in the common parts, meaning damage them, remove them or stop them working without a reasonable excuse. The accountable person can serve a contravention notice and may ask for the reasonable cost of repair or replacement. Residents must also be told regularly not to tamper with fire door closers.

question: Once we've finished a full refurb of the common parts, does the council's fire risk assessment need redoing?
reference_answer: Yes, it should be reviewed. The Order requires review when things have changed significantly, for example through alterations, or when there is reason to think the assessment is out of date. The LGA guide lists material alterations and completion of significant works as review triggers. Since October 2023 the whole assessment must be recorded, including the name of whoever helped carry it out.

question: What info does the council have to give residents about fire safety in the block generally?
reference_answer: In blocks with two or more flats, residents must be given understandable information on the risks the fire risk assessment found, the fire safety measures in place, the responsible person's name and UK address, who helped with the assessment, any nominated competent persons, and risks reported by other responsible persons. Separately, fire safety instructions covering the evacuation strategy and how to call the fire service must be displayed somewhere obvious and given to new residents and to all residents every 12 months.

question: Residents are asking whether they have to move out while we do the fire safety remediation on their block. What does the government guidance tell them?
reference_answer: The residents' guide says most people can stay at home while remediation is planned and done, and the owner, agent or landlord has to tell them whether staying is safe. Temporary measures such as temporary alarms, extra fire wardens or a changed evacuation plan may be used. Residents may have to move out for a while if the fire risk is serious, if urgent work cannot be done safely with people living there, or if the fire service or council judges the building unsafe.

reference_answer: Not under regulation 38. It covers building work that erects or extends a relevant building or is part of a relevant change of use. Circular 01/2025 took the words 'material alteration' out of paragraph 17.1 because that falls outside regulation 38. question: We built an extension onto a block of flats. When do we hand over the fire safety info, who to, and what goes in it?
reference_answer: The builder must hand the fire safety pack over to the responsible person by completion, or by first occupation if that comes earlier and the extension was empty during the work. The responsible person must confirm receipt, and the builder then notifies the building control body within 5 days (30 days under a self-certification scheme). It should include as-built plans showing escape routes, fire-resisting construction, fire doors and self-closers, detection and alarm equipment, any sprinklers and smoke control, plus equipment specifications and maintenance schedules.

question: New evacuation lifts are going into a block design. Where does AD B want them put?
reference_answer: Since the 2026 amendments, an evacuation lift should sit in an evacuation shaft that also holds a protected stair and an evacuation lift lobby. The lobby acts as a refuge, opens straight onto the protected stair, and must not open directly from flats, storage or electrical rooms. Any smoke control protecting the stair should give the lift and its lobby the same protection.

question: Electric meters on the landings of a single-stair block, is that OK?
reference_answer: A protected stairway should hold nothing but the stair, apart from a lift shaft or the electric meters. In single-stair buildings the meters should sit in cupboards that are kept locked and are walled off from the escape route with fire-resisting construction.

question: Is this block higher-risk?
reference_answer: I need the height from ground to the top storey's floor, the number of storeys (not counting basements or plant-only roof storeys), how many homes it has, what it is used for (flats, care home, hospital, hotel), whether it is joined to other structures, and whether you mean during building work or once occupied. In general a building in England is higher-risk if it is 18m or taller or has 7 or more storeys and has two or more homes; for building work, care homes and hospitals also count.

question: What fire rating does this door need?
reference_answer: It depends where the door is and whether this is new building work. Examples from AD B Table C1: a flat front door onto a common corridor or lobby is 30 minutes with smoke seals (E 30 Sa / FD 30S); a door inside a flat's protected hallway is 20 minutes; a door into a protected stair is 30 minutes with smoke seals; a lift or service shaft door is half the wall's rating, at least 30 minutes; a door in a wall between buildings matches the wall, at least 60 minutes. Tell me the door's position, the building type and whether it is new work or a check on an existing door.

question: Do we need sprinklers on this job?
reference_answer: I need to know whether it is a new building, an extension or a repair, how high the top floor is, and what the building is used for. For blocks of flats AD B recommends sprinklers throughout when the top storey is over 11m; new care homes need them whatever their height since the 2025 amendments; an extension that adds flats above 11m will usually need them in the new part. Repairs that are not building work do not trigger AD B on their own, but the fire risk assessment may still call for measures.

question: How often do the fire doors need checking?
reference_answer: It depends on the building's height and the kind of door. In blocks of flats with a top storey above 11m, flat front doors should be checked yearly (best endeavours) and communal fire doors, including riser and plant room doors, every 3 months at most. Below 11m the regulations set no interval, but the responsible person must still keep doors adequate under the Order. Tell me the height and type of building.

question: Is this fire stopping acceptable?

question: Roughly what should we price per FD30S flat entrance doorset, supply and fit?

question: What cable size and protective device should the sparks use for the sprinkler pump supply under BS 7671?
reference_answer: Not covered. AD B points to BS 9251 and BS EN 12845 for sprinklers but gives no wiring sizes or protective device settings. You would need BS 7671 and the sprinkler and pump standards themselves, or the system designer.

question: How do I size the pipework and water tank for a BS 9251 sprinkler system in a 12-storey block?
reference_answer: The documents only say sprinklers in residential blocks should follow BS 9251; they do not give hydraulic design, pipe sizes or tank volumes for that standard. You would need BS 9251 itself and a sprinkler designer.

question: Council wants a waking watch while the cladding comes off. How many wardens per floor do we need?
reference_answer: The residents' guide only mentions extra fire wardens as a possible temporary measure; none of these documents set staffing numbers for a waking watch. You would need the specific waking watch guidance (for example from the National Fire Chiefs Council) and the building's fire risk assessment.
label_note: out of scope

question: Do we need planning permission to replace the windows on a council block in a conservation area?
reference_answer: Planning permission is not covered by these fire safety documents. You would need the planning rules and to check with the local planning authority.

question: Which brand of intumescent pipe collar is best value for 110mm soil pipes?
reference_answer: The documents do not recommend brands or compare prices. AD B only says to use a proprietary seal that has been fire tested and keeps the wall or floor's rating, so you would need manufacturers' test evidence and supplier prices.
label_note: out of scope

question: Is there a compulsory qualification or card our joiners need before they can fit fire doors?
reference_answer: These documents do not set a compulsory qualification or card for fire door installers; they only say work should be done by competent people and mention third-party certification schemes in general. You would need industry scheme rules or specific competence guidance to answer this.
label_note: out of scope

question: New Awaab's Law job just came in. Can you run me through every deadline we're up against from the minute the tenant rings?
reference_answer: If there are grounds to think it is an emergency, the investigation and any make-safe work must both be finished inside 24 hours, starting when the landlord first knows. Otherwise a competent investigator must finish the investigation inside 10 working days, with day 1 being the next day after it learns of the issue. The tenant gets a written summary within 3 working days after the investigation ends, unless all required work is already finished. For a significant hazard the make-safe work is due inside 5 working days once the investigation is over; preventative work must start (or steps be taken to start it) within 5 working days, actually start within 12 weeks and finish within a reasonable period. If the home cannot be made safe in time, the household must be offered suitable alternative accommodation at the landlord's cost.

question: Emergency hazard on an Awaab job, say water pouring through a ceiling. How fast do we have to get there and finish, and when does the clock actually start?
reference_answer: The landlord has 24 hours to get the hazard investigated and finish any make-safe work the investigation calls for. Unlike the other Awaab timeframes, which start the day after the trigger, the 24 hours starts the moment the landlord has good reason to think an emergency hazard exists. If another law sets a shorter timeframe for the same repair (for example the council Right to Repair rules), the shorter one applies.

question: What actually makes damp and mould 'significant' under Awaab's Law, compared with a bit of mould we'd just stick on the normal repairs list?
reference_answer: A significant hazard is one a reasonable landlord, knowing the household's health and circumstances, would deal with inside 15 working days, though not as fast as 24 hours. The triage guidance treats damp and mould as significant where the people living there are likely to suffer serious health effects, including existing conditions getting worse, if it is not dealt with in time; it becomes an emergency where someone is particularly vulnerable or already has symptoms, such as a child whose asthma is affected. Small isolated patches, like mould on grout or sealant with no wider problem and no likely serious harm, are normally out of scope. Extent, which room, how long it has been there and ventilation and insulation also count; there are no fixed thresholds.

question: Tenant reported damp late on a Friday. Does the Saturday count towards the 10 days for the investigation, and which day is day one?
reference_answer: Only working days count: weekends, Christmas Day, Good Friday and English and Welsh bank holidays are left out. Day 1 is the first day following the day the landlord learned of it, so for a Friday report day 1 is the following Monday (unless it is a bank holiday), so the investigation has to be finished by the end of the tenth working day.

question: What has to go in the written summary we send the tenant after an inspection, and how long do we get to send it?
reference_answer: It must go within 3 working days, with day 1 being the first day after the investigation ends. It must say whether the investigation found a significant or emergency-level hazard and what it is; if more action is needed under the rules, what that action is with target dates to start and finish; if no more action is needed, that fact and the reasons; and how the tenant can contact the landlord. The target dates are not legally binding, but the tenant must be kept informed about timing and progress.

question: We went out the same day to a burst waste pipe, replaced it and cleaned up, all done. Do we still have to send the tenant a written summary?
topic: when a written summary is not needed
reference_answer: No. If the investigation identified required work and all of it, both making safe and stopping it coming back, was finished within the 3 working day window, no written summary is required. The tenant must still be told the work is complete, and the landlord should keep a record of the repair. If only the make-safe was done and preventative work is still outstanding after 3 working days, a summary is needed.

question: We assessed a mould report off the tenant's photos and said it wasn't serious. Now she wants someone to physically come round. Do we have to, and by when?
reference_answer: Yes. Where the earlier investigation had no physical inspection and no preventative work has started, the tenant's request triggers a renewed investigation that has to involve someone visiting in person and be finished within 10 working days, counted from the day after she asked. In effect the clock restarts. It is not needed if preventative work has already begun or if emergency safety work or a further investigation applies, though in a further investigation she can still ask for an in-person visit.

question: Inspection found the damp's coming through a damaged roof that needs scaffold, and we can't get scaffolders for about a month. Are we breaking Awaab's Law?
reference_answer: Not necessarily. The home needs to be safe inside 5 working days after the investigation, for example mould cleaned off and a dehumidifier supplied, and then kept in that safe condition. For the roof repair (supplementary preventative work) the landlord must either start within 5 working days or, if that is not reasonably practicable, take steps within that time, such as booking the scaffold and contractors, so the roof job begins as soon as it reasonably can and within 12 weeks at most after the investigation. The work must then be finished within a reasonable period.

question: If we can't make a significant hazard safe inside the 5 working days, what are we on the hook for with the family?
reference_answer: The landlord must arrange suitable temporary housing for the household, free to them, once the deadline for making safe has passed (5 working days for a significant hazard, a day for an emergency one) until the safety work is done or another end point applies, unless the tenant turns the offer down. Suitability depends on the household: number of bedrooms, distance to school and work, disability or medical needs, pets, and how long the stay will be. A hotel may be fine for one night but not for a six-week job.

question: Tenant won't move into the hotel we found while we fix a dangerous ceiling. Can she just stay put, and what do we owe her then?
reference_answer: Yes, the choice is hers, and once she refuses an offer the landlord need not keep offering (unless circumstances materially change). Because people are staying in the home, the landlord must give her a written document with safety advice by the make-safe deadline, or as soon as it reasonably can after that: what occupiers can do or avoid to reduce the risk, or a clear statement that nothing they do will bring the risk down to a tolerable level plus any steps that still help. The advice given should be recorded. Complaining that a place offered is not suitable does not count as turning it down.

question: When we rehouse someone under Awaab's Law, do we have to include her son who only stays over at weekends?
reference_answer: Usually yes. The household is the tenant plus family members who normally live there in line with the lease. A child under 18 counts if someone in the household has caring responsibilities for them and the child usually stays overnight at least once a week and would have kept doing so during the rehousing period.

question: Tenant keeps cancelling our damp survey. How much notice do we need to give to get in, and are we in trouble if we blow the 10 days?
reference_answer: The lease implies that the tenant must let the landlord or its authorised contractor in for Awaab work at reasonable times, with at least 24 hours' written notice. The landlord has a defence if it can show it used all reasonable endeavours, so keep a record of every attempt: calls, emails, letters, cards left, a choice of times, evenings and weekends too, and involving family or support workers. In extreme cases the landlord may consider an injunction after legal advice. In the end a court decides whether enough was done.

question: One of our lads spotted black mould in a bedroom while fixing a tap, and the mum mentioned her kid's chest is bad. Does the Awaab clock start when he saw it or when we tell the housing association?
reference_answer: The guidance says the answer turns on whether, in law, the contractor acts as the landlord's agent: if so, the landlord may be treated as aware when the contractor learns of it; otherwise awareness is when the contractor reports it. Landlords are told to take legal advice on this and to have clear processes so contractors pass on any hazards they see straight away. Contractors are expected to report hazards beyond the job in hand and give the landlord information for written summaries promptly. If the operative were the landlord's own employee, awareness would start when the tenant told him.

question: Does whoever does our Awaab's Law inspections need to be an HHSRS-trained surveyor?
reference_answer: No. Awaab's Law does not need an HHSRS assessment, so there is no HHSRS qualification requirement. The investigator must be a person the landlord reasonably thinks is skilled and experienced enough to judge if a significant or emergency-level hazard is present. Where relevant a properly qualified person should be used, for example a qualified electrician for an electrical hazard.

question: Housing officer reckons the mould's only there because the tenant dries washing on the radiators, so it's not an Awaab job for us. That's right, isn't it?
reference_answer: No. The guidance says landlords must not assume damp and mould comes from a tenant's 'lifestyle'. Cooking, bathing and drying laundry inevitably produce moisture and are unlikely to be a breach of the tenancy, so they are not a reason to skip Awaab's Law. Only hazards wholly or mainly caused by the tenant breaching the tenancy (for example deliberate damage or blocking extractor fans) fall outside it, and the landlord should investigate before deciding. A landlord that assumes lifestyle and does nothing risks breaching the law.

reference_answer: A hazard wholly or mainly caused by the tenant breaching the tenancy, such as blocking ventilation fans, is outside Awaab's Law. The landlord is still responsible for keeping the home safe under its other duties and policies and should think about how to support the tenant. If the investigation shows the real cause is a building deficiency, such as missing ventilation or poor insulation, it is in scope and the landlord must fix the root cause.

question: Heating in the block runs off a district system the freeholder looks after and it's gone down. Is that an Awaab job for the housing association?
reference_answer: No, provided the housing association has no duty to repair or maintain that system, because the hazard must come from a defect in something it must look after. The triage guidance gives exactly this case as out of scope. The landlord should still take reasonable steps to get it fixed, for example by raising it with the freeholder or management company.

question: Boiler's packed up in January at an 80-year-old's flat. Do we treat that as emergency or significant?
reference_answer: The triage guidance gives an elderly tenant whose boiler failed in cold January weather as an emergency hazard, meaning a 24-hour deadline to investigate and make safe. Over-65s and under-5s are at higher risk from the cold, and landlords should weigh the weather and whether any rooms can be heated. Temporary heaters can be used to make safe while the boiler is fixed. Broken boilers are also listed as a typical emergency hazard in the main guidance.

question: Tenant in her thirties says a patio slab in the back garden is loose. Do we need to deal with it on the Awaab timescales?
reference_answer: The triage guidance gives this case as out of scope: the chance of a fall is low if the area can be avoided and the tenant reported no vulnerabilities, so it goes through normal repairs. The picture changes if, for example, there are young children, people over 60 or someone with mobility problems, because their risk from falls is higher.

question: Our gas engineer found there's no working smoke alarm in a council flat with two little kids. Is that an Awaab emergency?
reference_answer: Yes. The triage guidance treats having no working smoke alarm inside the home as an emergency hazard (24 hours), and says it would likely be one whatever the household. Awaab's Law covers fire hazards within individual homes, for example a smoke alarm that is missing or broken, but not fire risks in the shared parts of blocks that fall under the Fire Safety Order. Separately, the smoke alarm rules require at least one alarm on each storey with living accommodation.

question: Fire door on a shared landing in our tower block is smashed. Do we log it as an Awaab's Law job?

reference_answer: No. Since the 30 November 2026 changes, fire risks caused by defects in the parts of a multi-home building that the Fire Safety Order covers are taken out of Awaab's Law: the structure, external walls, common parts and the doors between flats and common parts. Damaged communal fire doors are given as an example. These should be reported to the building's Responsible Person (or acted on if the landlord is the Responsible Person), and the fire and rescue authority enforces. Fire hazards inside individual flats are still covered.

question: EICR came back with just C3s and an old-style consumer unit, nothing damaged. Tenant wants the board swapped under Awaab's Law. Do we have to?
reference_answer: Usually not. A C3 means improvement is recommended but the installation is still satisfactory, and the electrical safety rules do not require the landlord to act on it. The triage guidance gives an undamaged consumer unit with only a C3 as out of scope, to be handled through planned improvement work. reference_answer: The triage guidance treats a damaged socket with accessible live parts and a young child in the home as an emergency hazard, so it must be investigated and made safe inside 24 hours. The investigation should be done by someone with the right skills and qualifications, normally a qualified electrician for this kind of hazard, who should also carry out the fix.

question: What actually changes for our repairs team on 30 November 2026?
reference_answer: The Awaab's Law amendment regulations take effect. Significant hazards widen from damp and mould to also cover excess cold, excess heat, falls, structural collapse, fire and explosion, electrical and domestic hygiene hazards (emergency hazards of almost any type have been covered since October 2025). The test for a significant hazard becomes whether a reasonable landlord would fix it inside 15 working days, replacing the earlier 'matter of urgency' wording. Fire hazards from Fire Safety Order regulated parts of blocks are excluded, and residential evacuation plan actions are not 'work'. On the same date the electrical safety rules switch to BS 7671:2018+A4:2026.

reference_answer: The phase 1 guidance said the remaining HHSRS hazards (except overcrowding) would be added in 2027. The phase 2 guidance says this will happen in phase 3 but gives no date, and the January 2026 Decent Homes statement expects the second and third phases within about two years. Emergency hazards of any type other than crowding are already covered, so a security or noise problem serious enough to need fixing inside 24 hours is already in scope, but non-emergency ones are not yet.

question: Tenant reports cracks in a 1960s large panel system block. Do we run that on the Awaab clock?
topic: structural collapse and large panel systems
reference_answer: Where the risk comes from building methods with known built-in weaknesses, for example large panel system blocks, and can only be made safe by large-scale structural work, a reasonable landlord could not fix it inside the 15 working day window, so it falls outside Awaab's Law. It still needs assessment and action under other laws, and tenant safety comes first. Cracks that appear suddenly or worsen fast, or other signs of imminent structural failure, can be emergency hazards, while superficial render cracks are normally out of scope but worth monitoring.

question: We're looking at a fire risk in a block with dodgy cladding. Is replacing the cladding Awaab work with the 5-day deadline?
reference_answer: No. Neither the make-safe work nor the preventative work under Awaab's Law includes cladding work. The landlord still has to meet the other Awaab duties: investigate, carry out any other safety work that is not cladding, and keep the tenant updated. Unsafe cladding is dealt with under the Fire Safety Order and, for high-rise buildings, the Building Safety Act 2022; interim options include changing the evacuation strategy with a waking watch, or alternative accommodation.

question: We do repairs for a housing association with general needs flats, some shared ownership, and supported housing where people are on licences. Which of those does Awaab's Law cover?
reference_answer: It covers social housing let on a tenancy by a registered provider, which includes general needs homes and temporary or supported housing where the occupier has a tenancy. It does not cover homes occupied under a licence, shared ownership or other low-cost home ownership, or long leaseholds. The tenant guidance notes some supported or temporary residents have licences, so the paperwork needs checking.

question: What should we be writing down on an Awaab job so the landlord's covered if the tenant takes them to court?
reference_answer: The guidance recommends clear records of all contact, investigations and communications with the tenant, including reports passed on by contractors or agents; tenant vulnerabilities, contact preferences and adjustments; every attempt to get access (calls, emails, visits, cards left); photos or samples of the hazard before work starts; the safety advice given; and correspondence with contractors and about alternative accommodation. These records are what the landlord uses to show it took all reasonable endeavours.

question: What makes something an HHSRS category 1 hazard rather than category 2?
reference_answer: The assessor judges the chance of harm needing medical attention in the coming year, assuming someone from the age group most at risk lives there, and the likely spread across four classes of harm, then a formula gives a score. Scoring 1,000 and above puts it in the High band, which is category 1; Medium (100 up to 999) and Low (below 100) are both category 2. Since the 2026 amendment these three bands replace the old A to J bands. Councils must act on category 1 and a power to act on category 2.

question: Our surveyors are still working off the old 29-hazard HHSRS list. Has that changed?
reference_answer: Yes, in England. The 2026 amendment merged several hazards so there are now 21, for example falls by baths and falls on flat floors now sit under one falls hazard, and hygiene, pests and sanitation became 'domestic hygiene'. Scores now fall into High, Medium and Low bands, and the harm classes are now named extreme, severe, serious and moderate (formerly Classes I to IV). The changes came into force on 23 June 2026 and apply to council inspections begun on or after 22 June 2026. Wales has its own rules.

question: Council EHO has slapped an improvement notice on one of the housing association's houses we maintain. How soon must the work start, and can they appeal?
reference_answer: Work cannot be required to begin until at least 28 days after service, and it becomes operative after 21 days unless it is suspended or appealed. An appeal goes to the First-tier Tribunal (Property Chamber) within 21 days of service and suspends the notice until it is decided. Not complying without reasonable excuse is an offence; for offences from 1 May 2026 the council can impose a civil penalty of as much as 40,000 pounds instead of prosecuting.

question: Can the council's own environmental health team serve an HHSRS notice on council houses we repair for them?
reference_answer: No. A council has no power to take HHSRS enforcement against itself as landlord, and the Court of Appeal has backed that view. It does not protect housing run by an ALMO, a tenant management organisation or another social landlord. Council tenants can instead complain to the council, contact a ward councillor or go to the Housing Ombudsman, and councils should still use the HHSRS on their own homes to make sure no category 1 hazards remain for the Decent Homes Standard.

question: Remind me what the decent homes criteria are that we're working to at the moment.
reference_answer: Under the current (2006) standard a home must: (a) have no category 1 HHSRS hazards; (b) be in reasonable repair, failing if a key component, or two lesser ones, are past their lifetime and in poor enough condition to need major work; (c) have reasonably modern facilities, failing only when three or more of these are missing: a kitchen no older than 20 years, a kitchen with enough space and layout, a bathroom no older than 30 years, a well-placed bathroom and WC, external noise insulation where needed, and adequate common entrance areas in flats; and (d) give reasonable thermal comfort through good heating plus adequate insulation. This applies until the new standard takes over in 2035.

question: Kitchen in this flat is 25 years old but in decent nick. That makes the place non-decent, so we've got to rip it out this year, yeah?
reference_answer: No. Under the current standard a kitchen over 20 years old is only one missing item on the modern facilities list, and a home fails that test only when at least three items are missing. For the repair criterion a component must be both past its standard lifetime (30 years for a kitchen) and in poor condition; age alone never fails a home. So a 25-year-old kitchen in good condition does not on its own make the flat non-decent.

question: How often do the electrics need testing in our social housing, and is there a catch-up deadline for tenants who were already in?
reference_answer: A qualified person must inspect and test the fixed wiring before each tenancy and then at intervals of 5 years at most, or sooner if the report says so. Where a social landlord's tenancy started before 1 December 2025, the first test of the wiring (plus checks of any equipment the landlord supplies) was due by 1 November 2026. The tenant gets a copy of the report inside 28 days, and the council within 7 days if it asks.

question: The housing association leaves a cooker and fridge in some of its flats. What checks do we have to do on those?
reference_answer: Equipment the registered provider supplies must be kept safe and checked by a competent person ahead of each tenancy and then at intervals of 5 years at most, or earlier if the last record says so, with a record (ISIT record) obtained each time. If an item is found unsafe the tenant must be told straight away and the item repaired or swapped promptly, with 28 days as the limit. Tenants' own appliances are their responsibility.

question: Void re-let next week. The EICR's three years old and the next-due date hasn't passed. Do we need a fresh one before the new tenant moves in?
reference_answer: No. The rules (clarified from 30 November 2026) count the pre-letting inspection as done where an inspection in the previous 5 years exists and its report's next-due date is still in the future. The new tenant must be given a copy of the latest report before moving in. The guidance recommends at least a visual check before the tenancy starts. The same approach applies to checks of landlord-supplied equipment.

question: We need to get the communal stairwell lighting covered by the five-yearly EICR under the electrical safety regs too, haven't we?
topic: electrical safety regs and communal areas
reference_answer: No, the Electrical Safety Standards regulations leave out shared parts of a block such as stairwells and corridors. The guidance still says shared electrics in a block should still be checked and maintained on a regular basis, and the council can take enforcement action about them under other laws, for example Part 1 of the Housing Act 2004.

question: EICR has come back with two C2s. How long have we got to sort them and what paperwork do we owe afterwards?
reference_answer: C1 or C2 codes make the installation unsatisfactory and the remedial work must be done within 28 days, or a shorter period if the report sets one. Within 28 days of finishing, the tenant (and the council) must get written confirmation from whoever did the work, such as a satisfactory EICR, an EIC or a minor works certificate. There is no breach where the landlord took every reasonable step where there was a real reason for delay, for example waiting for the supplier to fit an isolator. Where a specific tenant is at risk, Awaab's Law may require a faster response and the shorter timeline applies.

question: What does the landlord's basic repairing duty under section 11 actually cover?
reference_answer: The landlord must keep the structure and exterior in repair, which includes drains, gutters and outside pipework; keep in repair and working order the installations for water, gas, electricity and sanitation (basins, sinks, baths and toilets, but not appliances that use those supplies); and keep the space heating and water heating installations in repair and working order. For a flat this extends to parts of the building the landlord has an interest in and installations serving the flat, where the disrepair affects the tenant. The standard expected depends on the home's age, character, prospective life and locality.

question: Tenant's own washing machine flooded the kitchen. Do we have to repair the machine, and is any of it an Awaab job?
reference_answer: Neither section 11 nor Awaab's Law makes the landlord repair items the tenant can take with them, such as their own washing machine; section 11 also leaves out appliances that use the water or electricity supply. Repairs that fall on the tenant because they must treat the home in a tenant-like way are excluded too. Damage to the structure, such as the floor or ceiling below, still falls under the landlord's repairing duty, and if a building defect results in a significant or emergency-level hazard the Awaab rules can apply.

question: Tenant's solicitor reckons the flat isn't fit to live in. What will a court actually look at?
reference_answer: Section 9A, which the 2018 Act added to the 1985 Act, makes the landlord keep the home fit at the start and throughout the tenancy, including common parts it has an interest in. The court looks at repair, stability, freedom from damp, internal layout, natural light, ventilation, water supply, drainage and toilets, facilities for cooking and washing up, and any HHSRS hazard; an HHSRS assessment is not required. It can order works and/or compensation. Exceptions include problems caused by the tenant, fire or flood damage, the tenant's own belongings, and consents the landlord could not get despite reasonable efforts.

question: We're pitching for a stock condition survey contract. How often is a housing association expected to survey all its homes?
reference_answer: The Safety and Quality Standard requires a current, accurate condition record for every individual home, based on physically assessing each one. The Code of Practice does not fix a frequency: it depends on age, construction, archetype, complaints and repairs data. A rolling survey cycle over five years may suit some providers, but more frequent checks may be needed where there are lots of responsive repairs or recurring problems. Providers should use other visits, such as gas safety checks, to see inside homes.

question: Does the new regulator Competence and Conduct Standard touch us as a repairs contractor, or is it only the landlord's own staff?
topic: RSH competence and conduct standard and contractors
reference_answer: The standard (from 1 October 2026) is placed on registered providers, but it requires them to take appropriate steps to make sure the people working for their service providers, which can include contractors, are skilled, knowledgeable, experienced and behave well, and their written policy must say how they will do this. The qualification requirements only reach a service provider's managers where it runs a full housing management service for the landlord.

question: What's the proper way for our operatives to get rid of mould? Can they just blast it with bleach?
reference_answer: The guidance says to photograph and mark the area first, then remove the mould promptly with a mould and mildew product rather than bleach and let it dry fully. Wear goggles, gloves and a mask, shut doors to stop spores spreading but keep windows open, and bag and dispose of waste and cloths. Mouldy carpets, soft furnishings or ceiling tiles may need throwing away. Larger areas should be done by qualified professionals, and removing surface mould is never a substitute for fixing the cause.

question: How do we tell what kind of damp we're actually dealing with before we quote the fix?
reference_answer: The guidance describes condensation damp (the most common), penetrating damp from outside defects, rising damp from the ground (often misdiagnosed, best confirmed by chemical testing and often due to failed damp proof courses) and traumatic damp from leaks or flooding. It recommends an in-person inspection over photos, external checks (gutters, window seals, cracks, bridged DPC) and internal checks (staining, humidity, insulation, extractors, heating), and using qualified professionals, with thermography or monitoring in complex cases. There may be more than one cause.

question: My supervisor says under Awaab's Law we get 14 calendar days to go out and investigate a damp report. Is that right?
reference_answer: No. The 14 calendar day figure was the government's consultation proposal. After responses from landlords, the final rules use working days: a standard investigation has a 10 working day limit, with day 1 being the next day after the landlord learns of the problem. Emergency hazards have a separate 24-hour deadline.

question: Our surveyor scored the damp as only category 2 on HHSRS, so it can't be an Awaab's Law case, right?
topic: Awaab's Law does not need category 1
reference_answer: Wrong. A hazard does not need to reach category 1 for Awaab's Law to apply. HHSRS scores a notional vulnerable occupier, while Awaab's Law looks at the actual household's circumstances, so an older or unwell tenant may face serious danger from mould that only scores category 2. The test is whether a reasonable landlord, knowing the household, would deal with it inside 15 working days (significant) or 24 hours (emergency).

question: Tenant says the mould's making her baby wheezy. We need a GP letter from her before we can class it as an emergency, don't we?
reference_answer: No. Tenants do not have to provide medical evidence, landlords are not expected to be medical experts, and reports of vulnerability should generally be taken at face value (though evidence should be considered if offered). The damp and mould health guidance says action must not be delayed waiting for medical evidence. A young child already having symptoms points towards an emergency hazard in the triage guidance.

question: Flat's badly overcrowded and there's mould everywhere. Overcrowding isn't covered by Awaab's Law, so we can leave the mould to normal repairs?
reference_answer: No. Overcrowding itself is outside Awaab's Law, but other hazards made worse by overcrowding are not. Where the mould is serious enough to be a significant or emergency-level hazard, the landlord still has to make it safe and stop it returning within the Awaab deadlines, and use its allocations policy to help the household move to a suitable home.

question: Can the housing association recharge leaseholders in the block for the roof works, and what consultation does it need to do first?

You would need the service charge provisions of landlord and tenant law and the leases themselves.

question: Tenant rang to say the heating's off. Is this an emergency?
reference_answer: It depends. We'd need to know who lives there (older people, young children, pregnancy, health conditions), the weather and indoor temperature, whether every room is cold or some can still be heated, whether anyone has symptoms, and whether the system is the landlord's to repair (not, for example, a freeholder's district system). The triage guidance treats total loss of heating in cold weather with a vulnerable tenant as an emergency (24 hours), and a home that cannot be kept warm enough as a significant hazard.

question: How long have we got to fix this one?
reference_answer: It depends on what the problem is, who lives there and which rules apply. Under Awaab's Law an emergency hazard has a 24-hour deadline to investigate and make safe; a possible significant hazard investigated within 10 working days and made safe within 5 working days of the investigation, with preventative work started within 12 weeks. Other duties (for example remedial work after an EICR within 28 days) have their own timescales, and non-Awaab repairs follow the landlord's own published timescales. Tell us the defect, the household and the landlord type.

question: There's mould in the bathroom at a council flat. Is it an Awaab job?
reference_answer: Can't say without more detail: how big and how widespread it is, whether it is spreading beyond the bathroom, how long it has been there, the ventilation, who lives there and whether anyone's health is affected. The triage guidance gives an isolated patch over a shower in a home with no vulnerable occupants as out of scope (normal maintenance), while widespread mould with vulnerable or symptomatic occupants can be significant or even an emergency.

question: Does this flat pass Decent Homes?
reference_answer: We'd need survey details: any category 1 HHSRS hazards; the age and condition of key components such as walls, roof, windows, doors, boiler and electrics; kitchen and bathroom age and layout; noise insulation and common areas; and the heating type and insulation (loft and cavity). question: Do we have to put this family up somewhere else?
reference_answer: It depends. We'd need to know the hazard, the investigation result, the expected repair time and whether the home is a social tenancy. Where the problem falls outside Awaab's Law there is no rehousing duty under it, though other duties may lead the landlord to rehouse anyway.

reference_answer: Because he is not VAT registered, the VAT he paid on the tiles counts as part of his materials cost. question: VAT-registered painter sends £2,000 labour plus £500 paint plus 20% VAT on top. Do I take the 20% CIS off the VAT as well? And should he even be charging us VAT?
reference_answer: CIS is never taken from VAT, and for a VAT-registered sub the materials figure is also net of VAT. So the deduction is 20% of the £2,000 labour, which is £400.
