question: We held back £400 from a £2,000 invoice because the sub's work wasn't up to standard. Is the CIS worked out on £2,000 or £1,600?
reference_answer: Money you withhold because you believe the sub breached the contract is a set-off, and a set-off reduces the payment. So you take the 20% from £1,600 and show £1,600 as the gross payment on the monthly return. This is different from a contra charge (goods or services you supplied to him), which does not reduce the CIS figure.
label_note: set-off reduces the payment; example of 2,000 with 400 withheld

question: Releasing a 5% retention now on a job finished two years ago. Since then the sub has got gross payment status. Do I deduct from the retention or not?
reference_answer: Retentions follow the normal rules, and what matters is the sub's status on the day you pay, not the date of the work. Before releasing it, decide whether you need to verify him again (were you including him on returns in the current or last two tax years?). If HMRC confirms gross status, pay the retention gross.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 3.2 When a contractor has to verify a subcontractor
label_note: retention follows status at the date of payment; verification window

question: For the tax month ending 5 December, when does the CIS return have to reach HMRC and when do I have to pay the deductions over if I pay by bank transfer?
reference_answer: The return must reach HMRC by 19 December, 14 days after the tax month closes. Deductions paid electronically are due within 17 days, so by 22 December (19 December if paying by post or cheque); if the 22nd falls on a weekend or holiday, pay by the banking day before. You owe the amount you should have deducted even if you forgot to deduct it.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 4.12 Making payments to HMRC
label_note: return within 14 days; payment within 17 days if electronic, 14 otherwise

question: We didn't pay a single sub in October. Do I still have to send HMRC anything?
reference_answer: Yes. Since 6 April 2026 a mainstream contractor that has paid subs before must file a nil return by the 19th if it paid nobody in the tax month. The only way out is to tell HMRC in advance that you will pay no subs, at least 14 days before that tax month starts (an inactivity notice, lasting at most 6 months). If you do neither you get a late filing penalty.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 4.5 No return due for the month
hmrc-cis-340 section 4.18 Penalties for late monthly returns
label_note: nil return duty and advance notice exception, inserted from 6 April 2026

question: We missed taking CIS off one sub for three months, honest mistake. HMRC say we owe the 20% ourselves. Is there any way out of paying it?
reference_answer: The contractor is liable for deductions it should have made, but HMRC can direct that you don't pay the shortfall. You need to show you took reasonable care and the miss was a good-faith error (or you genuinely thought CIS did not apply), or that the sub was not taxable on the money or has declared it and paid his tax. If HMRC refuses, you can appeal within 30 days after HMRC's refusal.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 4.12 Making payments to HMRC
label_note: conditions A and B and the direction not to pay; the appeal is reg 9(7)

question: We're a limited company and the main contractors take 20% off us. How do we get that money back?
topic: CIS set-off for limited company subcontractors
reference_answer: A company sets the CIS taken from it against what it owes HMRC (monthly or quarterly) in PAYE, NI, student loans and CIS deducted from its own subs, and shows this on the EPS. Any surplus is carried forward within the same tax year. After the year end, once the final FPS and EPS are in, leftover deductions can be repaid or used against the company's Corporation Tax. Keep records of the set-off (form CIS132 can be used).
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 1.11 Subcontractors setting off deductions
label_note: set off via EPS against PAYE, NI and CIS; carry forward in year; refund after year end

question: Can we just put the CIS that main contractors took off us on the company's Corporation Tax return and claim it back that way?
topic: CIS set-off for limited company subcontractors
reference_answer: No. A limited company should not use its Corporation Tax return to claim its CIS deductions and risks a penalty for doing so. The deductions go through the payroll scheme: set them off on the EPS against PAYE, NI and CIS you owe, carry any surplus forward in the year, and claim a refund after the year end.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 1.11 Subcontractors setting off deductions
label_note: govuk text: do not use the Corporation Tax return, penalty risk

question: We're a company with two directors and want gross payment status. What turnover do we need to show?
reference_answer: HMRC looks at construction turnover for the past year, leaving out VAT and materials. A company needs £30,000 per director or £100,000 across the company; a company run by five or fewer people needs £30,000 per person. You also have to pass the business test (you do building work in the UK and the money goes through a bank account) and show your tax and NI have been paid on time.
cited_clauses: govuk-cis-subcontractor 'How to get gross payment status'
cis-regs-2005 regulation 27 Evidence prescribed to satisfy the business test
label_note: turnover 30,000 per director or 100,000; business test evidence

question: HMRC letter says we're failing the annual gross status review. How long have we got, can we appeal, and if we lose it when can we reapply?
reference_answer: You can first write back explaining why; if HMRC accepts it you keep the status. If not, they write again and the status goes 90 days later; you can appeal within 30 days of that letter, and an appeal holds off the cancellation until it is decided. After a normal cancellation you must wait one year to reapply. If it is cancelled straight away for false information, fraud or knowing failures (including the 2026 supply-chain fraud rules), the wait is five years.
label_note: write back, 90 days, 30 days to appeal, appeal holds off cancellation, 1 year wait

question: Heard that since April 2026 HMRC can make us pay if some sub-sub further down our chain dodges CIS or PAYE. Is that right, and how bad can it get?
reference_answer: Yes. From 6 April 2026, if you paid a sub and knew, or ought to have known, that someone in the chain on the same work was deliberately not deducting or paying over CIS or PAYE, HMRC can make you liable for a sum matching 20% of what you paid. A penalty of up to 30% of that amount can follow, and part or all of a company's penalty can be passed to a director whose actions caused it. Your gross status can also be cancelled with immediate effect, with a five-year bar on reapplying.
label_note: 20% liability for knowing payments; 30% penalty; immediate GPS cancellation and 5-year bar; officers liability

question: What actually changed in CIS from 6 April 2026? Give me the list for the office.
reference_answer: Three things. Mainstream contractors must again file a nil return for months with no sub payments, unless they told HMRC in advance. Money paid to councils and listed public bodies are no longer contract payments, so no verifying, deducting or reporting them. And new anti-fraud rules apply: liability where you knew, or ought to have known, about deliberate non-compliance in the chain, penalties up to 30%, immediate loss of gross status and a five-year wait to reapply.
label_note: simplification note lists nil returns and public bodies; fraud note lists the anti-fraud rules

question: We've paid the county council's highways team to do the road crossing into our site. I need to verify them and take 20% like any other sub, yes?
reference_answer: No. Since 6 April 2026 a payment to a local authority or one of the listed public bodies no longer counts as a contract payment. You should not verify them, should not deduct anything, and should not put the payment on your monthly return.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 2.11 Local authorities and public bodies as subcontractors
label_note: payments to s59(1)(b)-(k) bodies are not contract payments from 6 April 2026

question: Do I need to take the 20% CIS off the carpet fitter's invoice on the show flat?
reference_answer: No. Carpet fitting is one of the jobs outside CIS, so you pay the carpet fitter without a deduction. Vinyl, lino or laminate floors fitted to finish a building are inside the scheme.
cited_clauses: govuk-cis-contractor 'Construction work not covered by CIS'
hmrc-cis-340 Appendix C, C.3 Finishing operations
label_note: carpet fitting exempt; vinyl, lino, laminate included

question: We hire scaffolding from a firm that just drops it off, and on another job a scaffolder erects it. Which one is CIS?
reference_answer: Hiring scaffolding with no labour is outside CIS. Putting up and taking down scaffolding is a construction operation, so payments to the scaffolder fall inside the scheme.
cited_clauses: govuk-cis-contractor 'Construction work not covered by CIS'
label_note: scaffolding hire with no labour exempt; erecting scaffolding included

question: A labour agency sends us three labourers paid on timesheets at a day rate. Do we run CIS on the agency's invoices, and should they be reverse charging the VAT?
topic: CIS and reverse charge for labour agencies
reference_answer: If the workers do construction work under their contracts with the agency, it counts as your subcontractor and you apply CIS when you pay it; but if IR35 (off-payroll) rules cover the engagement, the payment is not a contract payment. For VAT, an employment business supplying workers (timesheets, hourly or daily rates, you direct the work) is supplying staff, not construction services, so there is no reverse charge and it charges VAT normally. A labour-only subcontractor that prices and is responsible for the work is different and is reverse charged.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 2.13 Rules for agency workers
hmrc-vatrevcon 'Scope of the construction reverse charge: Supplies of labour vs supplies of staff'
label_note: CIS part labelled; the VAT employment-business part is only in VATREVCON26000; relabel: added vatrevcon26000-top-text-1

question: Our client is a property investment company, not a builder, but it's spent about £3.5m on refurbs this year on flats it lets out. Should they be taking CIS off our payments?
reference_answer: Probably yes. A business outside construction becomes a deemed contractor once its construction spend goes over £3 million in a rolling 12 months. The own-property exemption only covers buildings used for its own business; property held for letting or as an investment does not qualify, so payments for that work are inside CIS.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 2.5 Expenditure incurred by certain businesses on their own property
label_note: deemed contractor over 3m (s59(1)(l)); own-property exemption does not cover let or investment property

question: Sub's invoice for first-fix plumbing on a shop fit-out has 20% VAT on it. We're both VAT registered, he's on CIS, and we bill the shop owner. Should it have been reverse charge?
reference_answer: Yes. Installing plumbing is a specified service, you are both VAT registered and you report his payment under CIS, and you aren't the end user, because you supply the work on to your client. Ask him for a corrected invoice marked as reverse charge. Even with the wrong invoice, it is your job to self-account for the VAT on your return.
cited_clauses: hmrc-vatrevcon 'Scope of the construction reverse charge: Services covered and not covered by the construction reverse charge'
hmrc-vatrevcon 'How the construction reverse charge works: End users and intermediary suppliers: End users'
hmrc-vatrevcon 'How the construction reverse charge works: Invoices: Invoices'
label_note: art 5(c) plumbing installation is a construction service; 2.1.2 conditions; end user definition excludes onward suppliers. Invoice correction part only in VATREVCON; relabel: added vatrevcon22000-top-text-1, vatrevcon33100-top-text-1, vatrevcon37100-top-text-1

question: Our roofer has gross payment status, so there's no reverse charge on his invoices, right?
reference_answer: Wrong. The supplier's CIS payment status makes no difference to the VAT reverse charge. If you are both VAT registered, the payment is reported under CIS and the work is a specified service, the reverse charge applies whether he is paid gross or under deduction.
cited_clauses: hmrc-vatrevcon 'How the construction reverse charge works: Who needs to apply the construction reverse charge: Gross Payment subcontractors'
hmrc-vatrevcon 'How the construction reverse charge works: Who needs to apply the construction reverse charge: Description of roles'
label_note: no usable section says gross status is irrelevant; inferred: conditions are VAT registration and CIS reporting, and gross-paid subs are on the CIS return; relabel: added vatrevcon32200-top-text-1, vatrevcon32100-top-text-1

question: Housing association client says they're an 'end user' so we should charge them normal VAT. What do we need from them before we stop reverse charging?
reference_answer: The end user exception only works if the customer confirms it to you in writing, no later than the supply or in the written contract. A letter, email or a clause in the contract will do; keep a copy to show HMRC. Once you have it, charge VAT as normal. Without written notice you should keep applying the reverse charge.
cited_clauses: hmrc-vatrevcon 'How the construction reverse charge works: End users and intermediary suppliers: End user notification'
hmrc-vatrevcon 'How the construction reverse charge works: End users and intermediary suppliers: End users'
label_note: end user exception only with written confirmation no later than the supply or in a written agreement; relabel: added vatrevcon33400-top-text-1, vatrevcon33100-top-text-1

question: Job is mostly fitting CCTV and alarms, but our sub also digs the trenches and puts in the concrete posts. Reverse charge or not?
reference_answer: Installing security systems on its own is outside the reverse charge. But if it is one supply together with specified services such as groundworks, the whole supply is reverse charged. If the specified part is no more than 5% of what the contract is worth, both sides can agree at the start to disregard it; that is optional and is not worked out invoice by invoice.
cited_clauses: hmrc-vatrevcon 'Scope of the construction reverse charge: Supplies where the reverse charge element is a minor part'
label_note: security systems excluded (art 6(i)) but part of a single supply with art 5 services is reverse charged (art 7); the 5% disregard is only in VATREVCON25000; relabel: added vatrevcon25000-top-text-1

question: We're building new houses for sale. Does our groundworker have to reverse charge us?
topic: VAT reverse charge and zero-rated new build
reference_answer: No. Groundworks done in the course of building new dwellings are normally zero-rated, and zero-rated supplies are outside the reverse charge because there's no VAT to shift onto you. It only covers standard-rated and reduced-rated services.
cited_clauses: hmrc-vatrevcon 'Scope of the construction reverse charge: Zero-rated supplies'
vat-notice-708 paragraph 3.3.4 Work closely connected to the construction of the building
label_note: 2.1.2 limits the reverse charge to standard and reduced-rated services; 3.3.4 groundworks for a new building are zero-rated; relabel: added vatrevcon27000-top-text-1

question: We knocked down a bungalow to ground level and are building a new detached house on the plot for the owner. Zero-rated or 5%?
reference_answer: It can be zero-rated. A building put up after the old one is flattened right down to ground level counts as a new qualifying building if it meets the dwelling tests: self-contained, can be used and sold separately, and built in line with planning consent. Your services must be part of the building works and not be excluded items (for example professional fees or plant hired without an operator).
cited_clauses: vat-notice-708 paragraph 3.4 Services excluded from zero rating
label_note: demolished to ground level then built from scratch; dwelling conditions; basic conditions

question: Building a granny annexe at the back of the client's garden. It can't be sold separately from the main house. That's zero-rated new build, isn't it?
reference_answer: No. An annexe that can't be lived in or sold on its own, apart from the main house, does not meet the 'designed as a dwelling' conditions, so building it can't take the zero rate; expect 20%.
cited_clauses: vat-notice-708 paragraph 3.2.2 Examples of when a qualifying building is not constructed
label_note: granny annexe that cannot be used or disposed of separately is named as not qualifying

question: Renovating a terraced house that's been empty for three years. Can we charge 5% VAT, and what proof do we need?
reference_answer: Yes, renovating a home nobody has occupied for at least 2 years before you start can be charged at 5%. Proof can come from electoral roll or council tax records, utility companies or the council's Empty Property Officer; a letter from that officer is enough on its own. Some items stay at 20%: carpets, fitted wardrobes, scaffolding, hire of goods, landscaping and professional fees.
cited_clauses: vat-notice-708 paragraph 8.3.2 Proof that the premises has been empty for 2 years
label_note: 2-year rule, proof incl. Empty Property Officer, which services are reduced-rated

question: The new owner moved into the empty house a few weeks before we started the refurb. Can we still do it at 5%?
reference_answer: Normally, if the house is lived in when the work starts, it is standard-rated. There is an exception for a single household dwelling: 5% can still apply if it stood empty for two years before the purchase, no renovation was done in that period, you supply the work to the owner directly, and the work is within a year of the purchase. A subcontractor on that job must charge 20%.
cited_clauses: vat-notice-708 paragraph 8.3.4 People living in the premises whilst you carry out the work
label_note: second empty house rule for single household dwellings (the rule text sits under para-8.3, not under 8.3.4)

question: Converting an old office block into four flats for a developer. What VAT rate do we charge?
reference_answer: Turning offices or other non-residential premises into homes, or altering how many dwellings there are, is a qualifying conversion at 5% for a normal developer. It would be 0% only if the conversion were done for a relevant housing association. Fitting non-building-material goods such as carpets stays at 20%, and work unrelated to the conversion cannot be reduced-rated.
cited_clauses: vat-notice-708 paragraph 7.3 Conversions into single household dwellings
label_note: office block to flats is a qualifying conversion at 5%; 0% only for a housing association

question: We're a sub on a new care home. The client gave the main contractor a zero-rating certificate. Can we zero-rate our invoices to the main contractor too?
reference_answer: No. A subcontractor working for a main contractor should not be given the certificate and must charge standard rate on work for a certificated building such as a relevant residential building. Only the main contractor's supply to the client may be zero-rated using the certificate.
label_note: subcontractor must not be issued a certificate and must standard rate

question: Fitting kitchens in new-build flats including fridge-freezers and dishwashers. Is everything zero-rated?
reference_answer: Not everything. On a zero-rated new build, building materials you fit take the zero rate, and kitchen units are ordinarily fitted items. Fridges, freezers, dishwashers and similar appliances are not building materials, so the goods are standard-rated, though your fitting labour on a 0% project may stay at 0%. A cooker only counts as a building material if it is made to warm the room or the water.
cited_clauses: vat-notice-708 paragraph 11.2 Goods 'incorporated' by a builder
vat-notice-708 paragraph 13.6 Electrical and gas appliances
vat-notice-708 paragraph 13.9 Examples of articles not ordinarily incorporated in dwellings
label_note: only building materials follow the zero rate; most appliances are not building materials

question: Our sub-contract has no payment terms written in at all. When do interim payments fall due and when is the final date to pay?
reference_answer: Where the contract is silent, the statutory Scheme fills the gap (England and Wales). For a job of 45 days or more, interim payments are due on the later of 7 days after the end of each period (28 days if none is set) or the payee's claim, and the final date to pay is 17 days after the due date. The final payment falls due 30 days after completion or the claim, if later. The payer must also issue a payment notice within 5 days of each due date.
cited_clauses: scheme-cc-1998 Schedule Part II paragraphs 2, 4 and 5
scheme-cc-1998 Schedule Part II paragraph 12 'relevant period'
label_note: due date later of 7 days after period or claim; final date 17 days; 'relevant period' 28 days default in para 12

question: We want to pay a sub less than his application because of defects. Contract doesn't say anything about pay less notices. What's my deadline?
reference_answer: A pay less notice has to say the sum you consider due and how you worked it out. Where the contract sets no period, it must reach the sub at least 7 days ahead of the final date to pay. Miss it and you owe the full notified sum.
label_note: pay less notice at least 7 days before final date when not agreed; contents in s111(4)

question: The main contractor never sent a payment notice within 5 days of the due date and now isn't paying us. What can we do?
reference_answer: If the payer misses its payment notice, you can serve your own notice stating the sum due and how it is calculated at any time afterwards; the final date to pay moves back by the number of days you were late. If your contract let you send an application before the due date and you did, that application already counts as your notice. The payer must then pay the notified sum by the final date unless it serves a valid pay less notice.
label_note: payee's notice in default; final date moves; application treated as notice in 110B(4)

question: Our sub-contract says we only pay the sub once the client pays us. Client hasn't paid, so we don't have to pay the sub yet, correct?
reference_answer: No. A clause making payment depend on you being paid by someone else has no effect unless the third party (or someone up the chain) is insolvent. With the clause struck out, the parties can agree other terms, and otherwise the Scheme's payment provisions apply, so payment is due on the normal dates.
label_note: pay-when-paid ineffective unless insolvency; Scheme fills the gap

question: Main contractor is way past the final date and hasn't paid. Can we down tools, and what notice do we have to give?
reference_answer: Yes, if the notified sum is not paid by the final date you can suspend some or all of your work. You must first give at least 7 days' written notice saying you intend to suspend and why. The right ends when you are paid in full; the other side must pay your reasonable costs of suspending, and the suspension period is added to your time to finish.
label_note: right to suspend, 7 days notice, ends on payment, costs and time extension

question: If we go to adjudication over an unpaid valuation, how long does it all take?
reference_answer: After you give notice of adjudication, the adjudicator should be appointed and the dispute referred within 7 days. The decision is due within 28 days of the referral; this can go to 42 days if the referring party agrees, or longer if both sides agree. The decision binds both sides until the dispute is settled by court, arbitration or agreement.
label_note: 7 days to referral, 28 days, 42 with referring party consent; binding until final determination

question: The job was only four weeks long, so the sub can't take us to adjudication, can he?
reference_answer: He can. The 45-day point only decides whether a party is entitled to stage payments. The right to adjudicate applies to any construction contract, however short (contracts with a homeowner living in the property are excluded from the Act).
label_note: right to adjudicate applies to any construction contract; 45 days only for stage payments; residential occupier excluded

question: District council job, estimated £180k of works. Their tender pack wants three years of audited accounts and a pre-qualification questionnaire before we can even bid. Are they allowed to do that?
reference_answer: For a regulated contract under the threshold, a council inviting tenders cannot filter bidders through a separate suitability stage such as financial or technical checks. That ban lifts for works contracts at or above £207,720 for councils (£135,018 for central government), so a £180k works job is caught. The council can still look at suitability when it assesses tenders. The ban does not apply to call-offs under a framework or to Welsh devolved authorities.
label_note: no separate suitability stage below 207,720 for council works (s85(3) tree already shows new values); guidance para 18 is in text-4, para 16 in text-3

question: Council in England is tendering a £1.2m school refurb. Is that a full Procurement Act contract or a below-threshold one, and what does that mean for us?
reference_answer: Since 1 January 2026 the works threshold is £5,193,000, so £1.2m falls below the threshold and the lighter Part 6 rules apply. Because it is above £207,720, the council may run a separate suitability check ahead of tenders. If it advertises the work, a tender notice for below-threshold work has to go on Find a Tender first, and a contract details notice has to follow the award.
label_note: works threshold 5,193,000 (Annex A row 10); above 207,720 a suitability check is allowed; tender notice rules in s87

question: Council's got a £25k repair job. Will it show up on Find a Tender, or do they just ring round?
reference_answer: For councils (not central government), a below-threshold contract only becomes notifiable at £30,000 including VAT. Below that nothing requires a tender notice or contract details notice, and the council can ask targeted suppliers for quotes. If it does advertise a notifiable contract, the tender notice has to appear on Find a Tender before anywhere else.
label_note: notifiable at 30,000 for non-central authorities; no notice required below (guidance para 23 in text-6; para 10 in what-has-changed-text-2)

question: Can our local council keep a small works tender just for local firms? We'd love that.
reference_answer: Yes, in England since the 2026 Order, councils and parish councils may reserve below-threshold competitions to suppliers based in the UK or in a local area. 'Local' means the council's own area, optionally with neighbouring counties or London boroughs, and this has to be spelled out in the tender notice or advert. 'Based in' means having substantive operations there, whoever owns you. They can also reserve competitions to SMEs. Central government bodies follow a separate policy.
label_note: reserve to local area or UK; local area defined in art 3(5); guidance para 12. Must be stated in the tender notice (art 3(8), procurement-regs reg 24(2))

question: How fast does the council legally have to pay our invoices on a below-threshold works contract?
reference_answer: Within 30 days, starting on the day they receive the invoice or, if later, the day it falls due under the invoice. That does not apply if they treat the invoice as invalid or dispute it, but they must tell you without undue delay if so. A valid invoice needs the minimum information the Act requires plus anything the contract asks for.
label_note: 30 days from receipt or later due date; disputed invoices; notify without undue delay; valid invoice

question: We're a sub on a big council contract under the Procurement Act. The main contractor's sub-contract says they pay us in 60 days. Can they do that?
reference_answer: Not if the council's contract counts as a public contract. The Act implies the 30-day payment terms into all public sub-contracts (one substantially for performing the public contract), and any term trying to override them has no effect, so 60 days cannot be enforced. Paying earlier than 30 days is allowed. This does not apply to sub-contracts under concession contracts, private utility contracts or school contracts.
label_note: 30-day terms implied into public sub-contracts; overriding terms of no effect

question: Council always pays us late. Is there anywhere I can see how quickly they actually pay?
reference_answer: Authorities have to publish their payments compliance notices on Find a Tender no more than 30 days after each six-month reporting period (periods run from 1 October and 1 April). It shows their average days to pay, the share paid within 30, 31 to 60 and 61+ days, and the share paid on 30-day terms. It is only required for public contracts; including below-threshold contracts is voluntary.
label_note: publish within 30 days of each reporting period; paras 11-12 (periods, contents) are in text-1; para 54 where published

question: Thresholds changed in January 2026, but the council published the tender notice for our job in December 2025. Which thresholds apply?
reference_answer: The old ones. The new thresholds from 1 January 2026 do not affect a procurement that had already started, and publishing a tender notice before that date counts as starting it.
label_note: new thresholds do not affect a procurement commenced before 1 Jan 2026; a published tender notice counts

question: What exactly counts as an SME when councils reserve tenders for small firms? We've got 30 staff and £6m turnover.
reference_answer: Under the Procurement Act an SME has under 250 staff, and either turnover of £44 million or less or a balance sheet of £38 million or less. With 30 staff and £6m turnover you are an SME.
label_note: para 21 (in definitions-text-1) defines SME: under 250 staff and turnover or balance sheet limits

question: If we bid for a central government job worth over £5m a year, what do they want to see about how we pay our own subbies?
reference_answer: Since September 2019 bidders for central government contracts over £5 million a year must show they have effective payment systems. The standard is that 95% of supply chain invoices are paid within 60 days, and firms that miss it could be stopped from winning government work.
label_note: bidders over 5m a year must show payment systems; 95% within 60 days

question: Last year a council terminated one of our contracts for poor performance. Could that get us excluded from future public tenders?
reference_answer: It can. Breaching a contract with a public body in a sufficiently serious way is a discretionary exclusion ground, and termination (or part termination), damages or a settlement count as serious. Failing to perform to the authority's standard after a proper chance to improve is also a ground. Discretionary means the buyer decides whether to exclude.
label_note: breach of contract and poor performance discretionary exclusion ground

question: We've never bid for public work. How do we get set up to see and bid for council tenders?
topic: Registering on the central digital platform
reference_answer: Register on Find a Tender, the government's central digital platform, which is free. Create a One Login account on GOV.UK, register your organisation as a supplier with your Companies House number (or get a platform identifier), and complete your supplier information such as connected persons, exclusions and financial details. Share your unique identifier with the buyer before award, and set up saved searches to get emailed about new tenders.
cited_clauses: procurement-supplier-guide 'How to register your organisation and find your unique identifier'
procurement-supplier-guide 'Searching for opportunities and setting up notifications'
label_note: registration steps, Companies House number, supplier information, free to use

question: What do I take off this new lad's money?
reference_answer: It depends on what HMRC says when you verify him, which you must do before the first payment if he is new to you. You need his UTR, his NI number if he is a sole trader (or company details), and his name exactly as registered. The result will be 20% if registered, 30% if not registered or not matched, or nothing if he has gross status, and the deduction only applies to the labour part after his own materials, hired plant and VAT.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 3.12 How to calculate the amount to deduct
label_note: rates 20/30/0 depend on verification; answers every reading

question: Is this invoice meant to be reverse charge or not?
reference_answer: Need more detail: what work it is for, whether both firms are VAT registered, whether the payment is reported under CIS, whether the work is zero-rated, and whether the customer has given written end user notice. It covers standard or reduced-rated construction services between VAT-registered businesses reported under CIS. It does not apply to workers supplied by an employment business, zero-rated work, supplies within a VAT group, or customers who have given written end user or intermediary notice.
cited_clauses: hmrc-vatrevcon 'Scope of the construction reverse charge: Background to and relationship to the Construction Industry Scheme (CIS)'
label_note: conditions for the reverse charge and the exceptions; relabel: added vatrevcon21000-top-text-1, vatrevcon21000-top-text-2

question: What VAT do I put on the house job?
reference_answer: Depends what the job is. Work on existing buildings is usually 20%. A brand new dwelling can be 0%, turning non-residential premises into homes or altering how many dwellings there are is usually 5%, and renovating a home empty for at least 2 years can be 5%. Tell me whether it is new build or existing, how long it has been empty, what the building was before, who the client is and whether you are main contractor or sub.
label_note: standard rate default and the list of 0% and 5% exceptions

question: When have I got to pay my sub?
reference_answer: First check what your sub-contract says about due dates and final payment dates; those apply if they are adequate. If the contract is silent, the statutory Scheme sets due dates and a final date to pay 17 days after each due date. If the job is a sub-contract under a Procurement Act public contract, a 30-day maximum from receipt of invoice is implied. Tell me the contract terms and the type of job.
cited_clauses: scheme-cc-1998 Schedule Part II paragraphs 4 and 8
label_note: contract must set due and final dates; Scheme gives 17 days if silent. The public sub-contract reading needs procurement-act s73

question: Does the council have to put this job out to tender?
reference_answer: It depends on the estimated value, whether it is works or goods and services, whether the buyer is a council or central government, and whether they are using a framework. Below the thresholds (works £5,193,000 from 2026) the council has wide freedom, including asking chosen suppliers for quotes or making a direct award, subject to its own rules. If it advertises a contract worth £30,000 or more, it must first put out a tender notice for below-threshold work.
label_note: threshold table decides; guidance para 14 on below-threshold freedom (in text-2)

question: Got a job in Glasgow with no payment terms in the sub-contract. What default periods apply up there?
reference_answer: Not covered. Part II of the Construction Act does reach Scotland, but the default payment rules in our documents are the Scheme for England and Wales only. You would need the Scottish Scheme for Construction Contracts regulations to answer this.
label_note: out of scope

question: What rate of interest can I charge a main contractor who pays us late?
reference_answer: Not covered by these documents. They deal with payment notices, due dates, suspension and adjudication, but not statutory late payment interest. You would need the Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 and the current reference rate, or what your contract says.
label_note: out of scope

question: We're bidding for a Welsh council job. What are the procurement thresholds in Wales now?
reference_answer: Not covered. The 2026 threshold changes we have apply to contracts other than those the Welsh Ministers regulate, and say Wales is making its own instrument. You would need the Welsh thresholds regulations or Welsh Government guidance.
label_note: out of scope

question: How do I tell if one of my regular labourers should really be on PAYE instead of CIS? What are the tests?
reference_answer: The documents say you must check whether someone should be an employee and that a wrong status on the return can cost up to £3,000, but they do not set out the status tests. You would need HMRC's employment status guidance (for example the Employment Status Manual or HMRC's status tool).
label_note: out of scope

question: Is there a legal cap on cash retentions? Main contractor wants to hold 10%.
reference_answer: Not covered. Our documents only say how retentions are treated for CIS and VAT, not how much can be held. You would need the contract terms and any specific legislation or guidance on retentions.
label_note: out of scope

question: What's the CITB levy rate this year and when do we pay it?
reference_answer: Not covered. VAT Notice 708 only explains the VAT treatment when a contractor withholds a levy contribution, not the levy rate or payment dates. You would need CITB's own levy guidance and the current Levy Order.
label_note: out of scope

question: Which CIS software is cheapest for a firm with about 20 subbies?
reference_answer: Not covered; the documents do not compare products or prices. They only say you can use HMRC's free CIS online service or commercial CIS software, and that verifying more than 50 subcontractors needs commercial software.
label_note: out of scope

question: When is our company's Corporation Tax due and what's the rate on our profits?
reference_answer: Not covered. The CIS documents only mention Corporation Tax for using leftover CIS deductions after the year end. You would need HMRC's Corporation Tax guidance for rates and payment dates.
label_note: out of scope

question: We're building a kitchen extension for a homeowner and it's only my firm on the job. Who counts as the client under CDM, and do I end up doing the client's bits?
reference_answer: The homeowner is a domestic client because the work is on their own home and not for a business. On a single-contractor job the client duties move to that contractor, so your firm carries them on top of its own contractor duties. HSE says in practice this means little more than managing the job safely as you normally would.
label_note: reg 7(1)(a) moves client duties to the single contractor; L153 App 6 para 3 and the HSE page say it is little more than normal; L153 para 54 sits in the reg 7 text block

question: Homeowner job, we're the main builder but the client has booked their own sparky directly. Does that change anything about who is principal contractor?
topic: CDM domestic client, more than one contractor
reference_answer: Once a second contractor is involved, the client should appoint, in writing, both a principal contractor and a principal designer. If a homeowner does not, whoever controls the building work automatically becomes principal contractor, and whoever controls the design stage becomes principal designer; that principal contractor then also carries the client duties, and because two or more contractors are involved the job also needs an H&S file.
label_note: reg 7(2) default PC/PD when homeowner does not appoint; reg 5(1) appoint in writing; App 6 paras 5-6; para 114 (H&S file) is in the file text block

question: Loft conversion, about six weeks with four of my lads on it. Do I need to send HSE an F10?
reference_answer: You notify only if the work is planned to run over 30 working days with over 20 people on site at once, or to total over 500 person days. Six weeks with four people is roughly 120 person days and never more than 20 at once, so it is not notifiable. CDM still applies in full, including the construction phase plan.
label_note: reg 6(1) thresholds; L153 para 52 (CDM applies anyway) is in the reg 6 text block; relabel: added cis80

question: On a big domestic job that does need notifying, is it the homeowner who sends the F10 or me? And do I have to stick it up somewhere?
reference_answer: For a domestic client the notification duty passes to the contractor (single contractor) or the principal contractor, or to the principal designer where that has been agreed in writing. Send it to HSE as early as you can before work starts, most easily with the online F10 form. A current copy must be displayed in the site office where workers can read and understand it, and updated if things change.
label_note: reg 7(1) passes the reg 6 duty to contractor/PC/PD; 6(2) timing; 6(3) display; L153 paras 49-51 in the reg 6 text block

question: One week bathroom refit for a homeowner. Do I honestly need a written phase plan for that?
reference_answer: Yes. Every construction project needs a construction phase plan, and on a single-contractor job you must draw it up before you set up the site. It should be proportionate: for small routine domestic work a short plan, such as the HSE busy builder template, normally does the job and shows you have planned for safety.
label_note: reg 15(5) single contractor draws up CPP before site set-up; L153 para 161 (busy builder template) is in this text block; relabel: added cis80

question: What do I actually need to put in the CPP for a small house extension?
reference_answer: The plan has to cover your safety arrangements and the rules for the site, plus specific measures for any high-risk work listed in Schedule 3. For a small job HSE suggests recording key dates, what the client told you (services, isolation points, any asbestos), the main dangers and controls (work at height, propping structures and excavations, dust and asbestos), where the toilets, washing and rest facilities are, other trades on the job, who is in charge and how supervision works. Keep it short and easy to understand.
label_note: reg 12(2) and App 3 paras 2-3 give the required content; the small-job checklist itself is in CIS80, which has no sections; relabel: added cis80

question: The homeowner's architect says they want to run the whole project and carry the client responsibilities rather than us. Is that allowed?
reference_answer: Yes. A homeowner can sign a written agreement so the principal designer carries the client role. Without that written agreement, the client duties pass automatically to the principal contractor, even if the designer is coordinating the project. Where the agreement exists, the principal contractor reports to that designer in place of the homeowner.
label_note: reg 7(1)(c) written agreement with PD; HSE page text-2 says without it duties go to PC; App 6 para 7; L153 para 55 in the reg 7 text block

question: A housing association has hired us to refurb some of their flats. They're people's homes, so the client duties fall on us like on a homeowner job, right?
reference_answer: No. Housing associations, councils, landlords and other businesses that own homes are not domestic clients under CDM. They are commercial clients and carry the client duties in full, such as arranging how the project is managed and passing on pre-construction information. Only a private person having their own or a relative's home worked on, not for a business, counts as domestic.
label_note: L153 para 53 (in the reg 7 text block) says housing associations, councils and landlords are not domestic clients; reg 4 commercial client duties

question: The job isn't notifiable, so CDM doesn't really apply to it, does it?
reference_answer: That is wrong. HSE's guidance says the CDM requirements apply whether or not a project is notifiable. You still need a construction phase plan, welfare, site induction and the other contractor duties; notification only adds the F10.
label_note: L153 para 52 (in the reg 6 text block): CDM applies whether or not notifiable; reg 15 contractor duties

question: What should a site induction cover for new lads starting with us on a job?
reference_answer: Every worker must get a site induction, from the principal contractor or from their own contractor if the principal contractor has not given one. It should be specific to the site and cover the particular risks and controls, an outline of the project and how it is managed, first-aid arrangements, how to report accidents, toolbox talks, how workers are consulted, and each person's own responsibilities. Workers must also be told what to do if there is serious and imminent danger.
label_note: L153 para 133 lists induction content; reg 13(4)(a) and 15(9)(a)-(b) induction and serious danger procedures; para 173 in the 171-supervisors block

question: Half my operatives are Romanian and some don't have much English. Do I have to give them the safety info in a way they actually understand?
reference_answer: Yes. Under CDM any information or instruction must be comprehensible, and under the Management Regulations employers must give staff information on risks and controls that is relevant and that they can understand. HSE's Romanian pocket card says employers must make sure workers have understood the training and safety signs and can always talk to an experienced supervisor they understand.
label_note: CDM 8(6) comprehensible information; MHSWR 10(1) comprehensible and relevant; the Romanian card has no tree (hse-romanian tree is only a list of leaflet titles); relabel: added ro-indg410

question: One of my Romanian lads asked if he can say no to going up on a scaffold he thinks is dodgy. Where does he stand?
reference_answer: HSE's Romanian worker leaflet says workers may stop work and leave the area if they believe they are in danger, and can raise concerns with the employer or HSE without getting into trouble. Employers must have procedures that let people down tools and get somewhere safe if serious and imminent danger arises. Workers must also report dangers they spot to the person in control.
label_note: MHSWR 8(2)(b) stop work and go to safety; 14(2) and CDM 8(5) report danger; the worker leaflet (best source) has no tree; relabel: added ro-indg450

question: Un băiat de-al meu m-a întrebat dacă are dreptul la pauză când stă 8 ore pe șantier. Ce spune HSE?
reference_answer: HSE's Romanian leaflet for workers says a worker is entitled to a rest break of at least 20 minutes when working more than 6 hours in a row, as well as paid annual leave. The same leaflet lists toilets, washing facilities, drinking water and first aid as basic rights. For working time detail it points to ACAS rather than HSE.
label_note: answer only in the Romanian worker leaflets, which have no tree; relabel: added ro-indg450, ro-indg410

question: What welfare do I need on a small domestic site? Toilets, washing, the lot.
reference_answer: You need toilets that are easy to reach, clean, lit and ventilated; basins with running warm water, or hot and cold taps, soap and towels next to the toilets; drinking water with cups if needed; a place to change and dry and keep clothes where special work clothing is worn; and a rest area with tables, chairs with backs, a way to boil water and to prepare and eat food, kept at a sensible temperature. HSE's busy builder sheet adds that basins should be big enough for washing forearms as well as hands.
label_note: CDM Schedule 2 paras 1-5 (toilets, washing, water, rest, changing); the forearm-washing detail is in CIS62/HSG150, no tree; relabel: added cis62, hsg150

question: Can we just use the homeowner's loo and kitchen instead of getting a welfare unit in?
reference_answer: CDM allows facilities to be either provided or made available, so using existing facilities can be acceptable if they meet the Schedule 2 standards and are readily accessible. HSE says that if you rely on facilities provided by someone else you should check they are suitable and kept in good order. Whatever you use must be in place before work starts and kept going until the job finishes, so agree it with the client first.
label_note: Sch 2 1(1) and 2(1) say provided or made available; L153 para 176 (in the welfare block) in place before work and kept to the end; HSG150 para 43 has no tree; relabel: added hsg150

question: Several subbies on site this month. Whose job is the welfare, mine as main contractor or each of theirs?
reference_answer: The principal contractor must make sure Schedule 2 welfare is in place for the whole build. Each contractor also has a duty, within what is reasonably practicable, for its own workers, so in practice subcontractors agree the arrangements with the principal contractor. Employers must also check the facilities are good enough for their own staff.
label_note: reg 13(4)(c) PC provides Sch 2 facilities; 15(11) each contractor; L153 paras 137-138 and 176-178 are in these text blocks; relabel: added hsg150

question: How many toilets do I need?
reference_answer: It depends on your headcount, how long the job runs and whether there is mains water and drainage. The law only says toilets must be suitable and sufficient and readily accessible, and HSE says the number depends on headcount. Where mains drainage is not possible, self-contained flushing units or chemical toilets can be used. Tell me the number of workers and the site set-up for a firmer answer.
label_note: underspecified; Sch 2 para 1 (suitable and sufficient, readily accessible) answers every reading; headcount guidance in HSG150 has no tree; relabel: added hsg150

question: Painting soffits and fascias on a two-storey semi, probably two days' work. Ladder or tower?
reference_answer: A ladder is allowed only where a risk assessment shows that better kit is not warranted, given low risk and either brief use or site features you cannot change. HSE treats short duration as roughly 15 to 30 minutes in one spot for light work, and says a tower or MEWP is often safer even for short jobs. Two days along the eaves points to a tower or scaffold, which also gives collective protection, preferred over personal protection.
label_note: Sch 6 para 1 ladder only if low risk and short duration; reg 7(1)(a) collective first; the 15-30 minute guidance is in HSG150, no tree; relabel: added hsg150

question: Someone told me ladders are banned on building sites now. Is that true?
reference_answer: No. HSE calls this a common misconception: often a ladder is the right piece of kit. The rule is that a ladder can be used when a risk assessment shows the risk is low and the work is short or the site cannot be altered, and it must be secured against slipping.
label_note: Sch 6 paras 1 and 5 show ladders are allowed with conditions; INDG401 (the misconception text) has no tree; relabel: added indg401

question: What angle should a ladder be at, how far does it need to stick out above the landing, and is footing it good enough?
reference_answer: Use the 1 in 4 rule: one unit out from the wall for each four units of height. An access ladder should be tied and stick up a metre or more past the landing so there is a handhold. To stop slipping, tie both stiles first; if that is not possible use a stability device or wedge the base; footing is the last resort.
label_note: law covers anti-slip and protruding; the 1 in 4 rule, 1 m and footing as last resort are in HSG150/INDG411, no tree; relabel: added hsg150

question: Is this ladder OK to use?
reference_answer: I need to know what the task is, how long it takes in one spot, the height, the type of ladder (trade or DIY) and its condition. In general a ladder is only for short, light work where better equipment is not justified; it needs a daily pre-use check and a recorded detailed inspection, firm level footing and no damaged stiles, rungs or feet. Household DIY ladders are generally too weak for site use.
label_note: underspecified; Sch 6 para 1 is the general test for any reading; checks and DIY ladder detail are in HSG150, no tree; relabel: added hsg150

question: How often does the scaffold have to be inspected, and what do I do with the inspection report?
reference_answer: A construction working platform someone could fall 2 m or more from must be inspected in position after it is put up and must have been inspected within the last 7 days, plus after anything that could affect its stability such as bad weather. The inspector must write a report within the same working period and hand it over within 24 hours. You keep it on site until the work is finished and then at your office for 3 months; Schedule 7 lists what it must contain.
label_note: reg 12(4) 7 days at 2 m or more; 12(3) after weather etc; 12(7) report same period and 24 h; 12(8) keep on site then 3 months; Sch 7 contents; relabel: added indg401

question: We keep shifting the aluminium tower round the room every hour or so. Does it need a fresh inspection every time we move it?
reference_answer: No. You do not need a fresh inspection and report each time a mobile tower is moved to another spot on the same site; it just needs an inspection on that site in the last 7 days. If guard rails or other parts are taken off to get past something, a trained user should do a pre-use check once it is put back, and a tag system can record that.
label_note: reg 12(4) mobile platform inspected on the site within 7 days; the guard-rail pre-use check and tags are in HSG150, no tree; relabel: added hsg150, indg401

question: It's only a couple of metres, so it's fine to push the tower along with my lad still up on the platform, yeah?
reference_answer: No. HSE says never move a tower with people or materials on it. Before moving it, bring it down to no more than 4 m, check for overhead lines and obstructions, and check the ground is firm and level with no holes.
label_note: only source is HSG150 para 164, no tree; relabel: added hsg150

question: Need to replace a few slipped tiles on a pitched roof. Do I have to put a full scaffold up for that?
reference_answer: Not necessarily. For a quick job on a pitched roof, decided on a risk assessment of things like pitch, condition and weather, the minimum is safe access up to the roof plus a purpose-made, supported roof ladder. It should reach across three or more rafters and be anchored over the ridge with a proper hook, not relying on the ridge tiles.
label_note: only source is HSG33, no tree; relabel: added hsg33

question: Customer's garage has an old corrugated cement sheet roof. My lad wants to walk across it to sort the gutter. OK?
reference_answer: Treat it as fragile: HSE lists unreinforced cement sheeting as likely fragile and says treat every roof as fragile until someone competent confirms it is not. You must keep people off and away from fragile sheets if the work can be done another way, for example from a tower or MEWP. If that is not possible, use platforms or coverings that take the load, measures to limit a fall, and warning notices. Old cement sheets may also contain asbestos, which these documents do not cover.
label_note: reg 9 fragile surfaces (avoid, platforms/coverings, fall limiting, notices); cement sheet as fragile is in HSG33, no tree; relabel: added hsg33, indg401

question: If a lad on a harness falls and is left hanging, do I really need my own rescue plan? Can't we just call 999?
reference_answer: Yes, you need a plan. Planning work at height must include emergencies and rescue. HSE warns against counting on 999 crews, who may be too slow or lack the kit, so agree a set rescue procedure and make sure workers know it.
label_note: reg 4(2) planning includes emergencies and rescue; the advice not to rely on 999 is in HSG150/INDG401, no tree; relabel: added hsg150, indg401

question: Cutting concrete blocks with a disc cutter today. What does the law expect me to do about the dust?
reference_answer: Block dust contains respirable crystalline silica, so you must assess the risk and prevent or adequately control exposure under COSHH. HSE's advice: plan to cut less or use a block splitter, stop dust getting airborne with water suppression or on-tool extraction, and give the right mask, properly fitted to a clean-shaven face. Exposure must stay below the silica limit of 0.1 mg/m3 as an 8-hour average, and RPE is used on top of other controls, not instead of them.
label_note: COSHH 6 assess, 7 prevent or control (7(3) hierarchy, RPE last); silica-specific advice in CIS78/CIS54, no tree; relabel: added cis78, cis54

question: What's the actual exposure limit for silica dust?
reference_answer: The workplace exposure limit for respirable crystalline silica is 0.1 mg/m3 averaged over 8 hours. HSE also notes that for carcinogens like this exposure must be reduced as low as reasonably practicable, not just kept under the limit.
label_note: silica WEL not in any current tree (hse-eh40 tree is only the product page); relabel: added cis54, eh40

question: I'll just clip a water bottle onto our 110V electric cut-off saw, water works on any saw for dust.
reference_answer: No. HSE says not to use water suppression on electric cut-off saws. For electric saws use on-tool extraction (LEV) instead; wet cutting is for petrol or other non-electric saws, with a flow of about half a litre a minute.
label_note: only source is CIS54, no tree; relabel: added cis54

question: Do my lads' dust masks need face-fit testing? One of them has a big beard and won't shave it.
reference_answer: Tight-fitting masks (half and full face) must be face-fit tested by a competent person, and retested if the mask or the wearer's face changes. The wearer must be clean-shaven where the mask seals, so a tight-fitting mask will not protect the bearded worker. A loose-fitting powered hood or visor does not need fit testing and is the usual option for someone with a beard.
label_note: COSHH 7 holds the general RPE duty but not face-fit testing or beards; L5 para 160 and CIS78 have no tree; relabel: added l5, cis78

question: We've got a dust extraction unit in the workshop. How often does it need a proper check and how long do I keep the paperwork?
reference_answer: Local exhaust ventilation must have a thorough examination and test by a competent person no less than once every 14 months. Keep a record of the examinations, tests and any repairs for a minimum of 5 years.
label_note: COSHH 9(2)(a) LEV every 14 months; 9(4) records 5 years; wood dust page repeats 14 months

question: Our joiner sands oak skirting most of the day and he's started wheezing. What are the limits and does he need health checks?
reference_answer: The exposure limit for hardwood is 3 mg/m3 over 8 hours (softwood 5 mg/m3, and 3 applies to any mix). Wood dust is linked to asthma and hardwood dust to nasal cancer, so use extraction, a fitted mask for very dusty sanding, and vacuum rather than sweep. He should get health surveillance: a baseline, then usually yearly questionnaire and spirometry run with an occupational health professional, with a health record kept for 40 years.
label_note: wood dust WELs 3 and 5 mg/m3; health surveillance programme; COSHH 11(1) surveillance, 11(3) record 40 years

question: 1930s house, the paint on the sash windows is flaking badly. How should we strip it?
reference_answer: Assume it may be lead paint, as lead was used in house paints until the 1960s and not fully removed until the early 1980s. Only strip if it is flaking or a risk; use a chemical stripper, wet sanding paper and extraction on the tool, keep hot air guns below 500 C and never use blowlamps or gas torches. Wear throwaway overalls plus an FFP3 mask, bag the debris, and give workers a proper large sink with hot or warm water to wash before eating, drinking or smoking.
label_note: only source is CIS79, no tree; relabel: added cis79

question: Is this dust dangerous?
reference_answer: It depends on what is being cut or sanded, for how long and with what controls. Concrete, brick, block and stone give silica dust; wood gives wood dust; old paint may contain lead; older materials could contain asbestos. In general HSE says regular breathing of construction dust can cause serious lung disease, and COSHH requires an assessment and controls such as water, extraction and fitted masks. Tell me the material and task.
label_note: underspecified; COSHH 6(1) assessment applies to every reading; material-specific sheets have no tree; relabel: added cis78, cis79

question: There's 15 of us. Do I have to have my COSHH and general risk assessments written down?
reference_answer: Yes. With 5+ employees you must write down the significant findings of your risk assessment and any groups especially at risk, and record your health and safety arrangements. HSE's COSHH guide says the same for COSHH assessments and recommends writing them down even for smaller firms.
label_note: MHSWR 3(6) and 5(2) record at 5 or more employees; COSHH 6(4) record at 5 or more; relabel: added indg136

question: My lads are on the breaker and kango for hours. What are the vibration limits?
reference_answer: For hand-arm vibration, action is needed from a daily exposure of 2.5 (m/s squared, 8-hour average), and 5 on the same scale is the limit that must never be gone over. HSE's points system makes this easier: 100 points a day is the action value and 400 points the limit. Workers at or above the action value, or at risk, must be under health surveillance.
label_note: reg 4(1) HAV 2.5 action, 5 limit; 7(1) health surveillance; the points system in L140 has no tree; relabel: added l140

question: At what noise level do I have to give the lads ear defenders, and when do they have to wear them?
reference_answer: At the lower action values (80 dB(A) daily, or 135 dB(C) peak) you must make hearing protection available to anyone who asks. At the upper action values (85 dB(A) or 137 dB(C)) you must provide it, mark the area as a hearing protection zone and make sure people wear it there. The limit values of 87 dB(A) and 140 dB(C), which take account of the protectors, must not be exceeded.
label_note: reg 4 action and limit values; 7(1) available on request; 7(2) provide; 7(3) hearing protection zone and wear

question: I haven't got a noise meter. How do I know if I need to do a noise assessment?
reference_answer: You must assess noise if anyone is likely to reach the lower action value. HSE's simple test: if people need to shout to talk at 2 m for over about 2 hours a day, the level is probably around 85 dB(A) and an assessment is needed. Using loud power tools for over a quarter of an hour daily, or working in construction or demolition, are also signs you need to act.
label_note: reg 5(1) assess at the lower action value; the shout-at-2 m test is in L108, no tree; relabel: added l108

question: I'll just buy the ear defenders with the highest rating, the more they block the better.
reference_answer: Not quite. Hearing protection must bring exposure below the limit values, but HSE advises aiming for 70 to 80 dB(A) reaching the ear and avoiding anything that takes it below 70 dB(A). Over-protection stops people hearing traffic, plant and warning signals and makes communication harder.
label_note: reg 7(4) selection; the 70-80 dB(A) over-protection advice is in L108 para 83, no tree; relabel: added l108

question: First aid on a site with about 15 of us: what kit do I need and how many first aiders?
reference_answer: Every site needs a first-aid box stocked for the number of workers, a named person who takes charge of first aid, and a notice telling people who the first aider is and where. HSE's construction guide suggests at least one trained first aider for 5 to 50 people, with cover for shifts and weekend work. You must also arrange contact with outside emergency services. HSE's current first aid guidance (L74, amended 2024) says to base provision on a needs assessment, including mental health.
label_note: MHSWR 9 external services; L74 product page mentions needs assessment incl mental health; first-aid numbers are in HSG150, no tree; relabel: added hsg150

question: One of the lads broke his wrist falling off a stepladder this morning. Do I have to report it to HSE?
reference_answer: Yes. A broken bone other than a finger, thumb or toe is a specified injury and is reportable. Report it online, or by phone to the Incident Contact Centre, which takes fatal and specified injuries. Also keep a record of it, for example in your accident book.
label_note: only source is INDG453, no tree; relabel: added indg453

question: Lad hurt his back lifting blocks and has been off five days so far. Is that reportable?
reference_answer: Not yet. Injuries are reportable when the worker is off or unable to do normal work for over seven consecutive days, leaving out the accident day itself. You must record it now because it is over three days, and an accident book entry is enough; report it if the absence goes past seven days.
label_note: only source is INDG453, no tree; relabel: added indg453

question: The HSE toolkit for small builders says I must report anyone off work more than three days after an accident. So I'm reporting this one?
reference_answer: That toolkit (INDG344, 2008) is out of date on this point. Since RIDDOR 2013, the trigger is over seven days off, excluding the day it happened. Over-three-day injuries still have to be recorded, but not reported.
label_note: INDG453 and INDG344 have no tree; relabel: added indg453, indg344

question: Neighbour's kid tripped over our materials on the pavement and got taken to A&E with a cut head. Is that one for HSE?
reference_answer: Yes. An accident to a passer-by or other non-worker is reportable when they are injured and taken from the scene to hospital for treatment of that injury; you do not need to find out what treatment they got. It would not be reportable if they went only as a precaution with no visible injury. You also have a general duty not to endanger passers-by from your work.
label_note: only the general duty to non-employees has a tree; the RIDDOR rule is in INDG453, no tree; relabel: added indg453

question: Digger arm touched the overhead line at the back of the site. Nobody hurt, thank God. Do I need to tell anyone, and how far should we have stayed away?
reference_answer: Yes. Plant or equipment touching overhead power lines is a reportable dangerous occurrence even if no one is injured. HSE's busy builder advice is to keep plant at least 15 m plus the jib length from lines on steel towers, and 9 m plus jib length from lines on wooden poles, or get the line made dead, diverted or shrouded. CDM requires lines to be diverted or isolated, or barriers and warning notices where that is not practicable.
label_note: CDM 25(2)-(3) divert/isolate or barriers and notices; reportability and distances are in INDG453/CIS65, no tree; relabel: added indg453, cis65

question: Before we dig the footings, what do I have to do about buried cables and gas pipes?
reference_answer: Work that could strike buried services must not begin until you have taken suitable precautions. Get service plans from the utilities or site owner, locate the services with a cable avoidance tool, and mark the route with paint or pegs. Keep mechanical diggers and power tools at least 0.5 m away from the suspected route, and take care breaking through paving above services.
label_note: CDM 25(4) no work until precautions taken; plans, CAT and 0.5 m are in CIS65/HSG47 (hse-hsg47 tree is only the product page); relabel: added cis65, hsg47

question: Can the lads plug their 230V tools straight into the house sockets?
reference_answer: HSE prefers cordless tools or a 110V centre-tapped supply, which greatly cuts the risk of a fatal shock. If mains 230V tools have to be used, they must be plugged into sockets protected by an RCD rated at 30 mA or less with no delay, tested daily with its button. HSE also recommends a separate temporary site supply rather than relying on the existing house circuits.
label_note: HSG150 and HSG141 have no tree; relabel: added hsg150, hsg141

question: The customer's electrician says that circuit's switched off. Can my lad just crack on and chase the wall?
reference_answer: A verbal assurance is never enough. Once isolated, the circuit must be proved dead before work by someone competent using proper test equipment, such as a two-pole voltage detector tested before and after use; volt sticks and multimeters are not recommended for this. Precautions must also stop it being switched back on during the work, for example locking off. If you do not know where cables run, turn the supply off before drilling.
label_note: EAWR 13 stops dead equipment becoming live (locking off); proving dead is in HSG85/HSG141, no tree; relabel: added hsg85, hsg141, cis65

question: When is anyone allowed to work on live electrics?
reference_answer: Only when all three conditions are met: it is unreasonable in the circumstances for the equipment to be dead, it is reasonable for the person to do the job live, and proper precautions, including protective equipment if needed, are in place. If any one is not met, the work must be done dead. The person must also have the knowledge or supervision needed to prevent danger.
label_note: EAWR 14 three conditions for live work; 16 competence; relabel: added hsg85

question: My plumber does a bit of gas work on our jobs. Does he have to be Gas Safe, and is it on me to check?
reference_answer: Everyone doing gas work needs to be competent, and a self-employed gas engineer, or the firm employing one, must belong to the class of persons HSE has approved, which is currently the Gas Safe Register. As the firm controlling the work, you must also take reasonable steps to check he is registered, for example his Gas Safe ID card, which shows the types of work he can do. The duty to ensure competence extends to contractors who control the work.
label_note: GSIUR 3(3) approved class (Gas Safe); 4 controller checks; 3(1)-(2) competence; L56 tree is partial (paras 1-20 only); relabel: added l56

question: Customer wants the new gas boiler put in the en-suite. Any rule against that?
reference_answer: A gas appliance may only be installed in a bathroom or shower room if it is room-sealed. The installation must be done by a Gas Safe registered engineer.
label_note: GSIUR 30(1) only room-sealed in a bathroom or shower room; 3(3) registered

question: We're knocking through a wall in a flat and suddenly smell gas. What do we do?
reference_answer: Open doors and windows and turn the gas off at the meter valve straight away. If gas still escapes or the smell stays, call the National Gas Emergency Service (0800 111 999) at once. The supply must not be turned back on until the cause is fixed, and a Gas Safe engineer must do the repairs.
label_note: GSIUR 37(2) shut off, 37(3) notify supplier, 37(4) not re-opened until fixed; the emergency number is in INDG285, no tree

question: Is my plumber allowed to do this gas job?
reference_answer: I need to know what the job is (new appliance, pipework, servicing, or just swapping a cylinder hose), whether he is Gas Safe registered, and what work categories are on the back of his ID card. In general, work on gas fittings needs a competent person working for a Gas Safe registered business, with only small exceptions such as like-for-like hose or regulator swaps on portable heaters and cylinders.
label_note: underspecified; GSIUR 3 (competence and Gas Safe class, with exceptions) answers every reading; relabel: added l56

question: Do I need a written health and safety policy now we've got 15 on the books?
reference_answer: Yes. Employers must prepare a written statement of their health and safety policy and how it is organised and put into practice, keep it up to date and bring it to all employees' attention. With five or more employees you must also record your health and safety arrangements and the significant findings of your risk assessments.
label_note: HSWA 2(3) written policy; MHSWR 5(2) and 3(6) records at 5 or more

question: A few of my lads are paid self-employed through CIS. Am I still responsible for their safety on site?
reference_answer: Yes. HSE notes that a worker who is self-employed for tax can still count as your employee for safety law, and either way you must protect people working under your control. Under CDM a contractor has to plan, manage, monitor and supervise work done by workers under its control, and employers must not put people outside their employment at risk.
label_note: CDM 15(2) and 15(8) workers under control; HSWA 3(1); the self-employed-for-tax point is in INDG344, no tree; relabel: added indg344

question: Everyone does it: I'll take twenty quid out of the new lad's first wage for his hard hat and hi-vis.
reference_answer: You can't. An employer must not charge employees for anything provided because a specific health and safety requirement demands it, which covers required protective equipment. HSE's Romanian card for workers also says protective equipment must be given free where needed.
label_note: HSWA s9 no charge for things required by statutory provisions; relabel: added ro-indg410

question: Taking on a 17-year-old apprentice next month. Anything extra I need to do?
reference_answer: Before employing a young person you must make or review a risk assessment that looks closely at their lack of experience, their limited sense of risk and their age, the equipment they will use and the training they get. They must be trained when they start, and HSE's CDM guidance says young or inexperienced workers need closer supervision.
label_note: MHSWR 3(4)-(5) young person assessment; 13(2) training on recruitment; L153 para 170 (closer supervision) is in this text block

question: What training do my workers actually need for CDM? Do they all need cards and courses?
reference_answer: CDM says you must not put someone on site unless they have, or are working towards, the right skills, know-how, training and experience for the tasks. HSE suggests comparing what each worker already has with what the job needs and training to fill the gap; if they already show the right abilities, no more training is needed. Employers must also train staff when they start and when risks change, for example new equipment or new duties.
label_note: CDM 15(7) skills, knowledge, training, experience; L153 paras 165-167 in this text block; MHSWR 13(2)

question: We've got a 1.5 m trench with trench boxes in. Who has to inspect it and how often?
reference_answer: A competent person must inspect a supported excavation at the start of each shift, after anything that could weaken it, and after any material falls in, and must be satisfied it is safe before work goes on. If they are not satisfied, they must tell you within that shift and give a written report within 24 hours, which you keep on site and then for 3 months. You must also stop people, plant and materials falling in.
label_note: 22(4) inspection at start of shift and after events; 24(1) tell within shift and report; 24(3) keep on site then 3 months; 22(2) prevent falls in

question: Do I need to notify this job?
reference_answer: I need the planned length of the build, the most people working at the same time, and the total person days. Notification is needed if it runs over 30 working days with over 20 people at once, or exceed 500 person days. Every day work happens counts, including weekends.
label_note: underspecified; reg 6(1) thresholds answer every reading; L153 paras 47-48 (weekends count) are in the reg 6 text block

question: Do I need planning permission for a 4 m single-storey rear extension on a semi?
reference_answer: The health and safety documents here do not cover planning permission or permitted development. You would need the planning rules (the permitted development order) or advice from the local planning authority.
label_note: out of scope

question: We've got a job coming up in Edinburgh. What's the building warrant process there?
reference_answer: These documents do not cover Scottish building warrants or building standards. You would need the Scottish building standards guidance or the local council's building standards service. Site health and safety law such as CDM does apply across Great Britain, but the warrant process is separate.
label_note: out of scope

question: How much is a PASMA tower course and where can my lads do one near Luton?
reference_answer: Course prices and providers are not covered. HSE's guidance only says towers should be put up by trained, competent people using the PASMA-recognised methods. You would need to ask PASMA or local training providers.
label_note: out of scope

question: What size cable and breaker do I need for a new kitchen ring main under BS 7671?
reference_answer: Cable sizing and circuit design under BS 7671 are not in these documents; HSE's guidance only refers to BS 7671 for low-voltage requirements. You would need the wiring regulations themselves or a qualified electrician.
label_note: out of scope

question: How much employers' liability cover do I need, and does it have to cover my self-employed subbies too?
reference_answer: These documents do not set out the required level of employers' liability cover or who it must include. HSE's Romanian worker card only says employers must display their compulsory insurance certificate. You would need the employers' liability insurance law and guidance or an insurer.
label_note: out of scope

question: What's the minimum hourly rate I have to pay a first-year apprentice labourer?
reference_answer: Pay rates are not covered by these health and safety documents. HSE's worker leaflets point to ACAS for employment terms; you would need the current National Minimum Wage rates from GOV.UK.
label_note: out of scope

question: Do I need a permit from the council to put a skip on the road outside the customer's house?
reference_answer: Skip permits on the highway are not covered by these documents. You would need the local highway authority's rules; usually the skip hire firm arranges the permit.
label_note: out of scope

question: Which make of dust extractor should I buy for our 110V cut-off saws, and roughly what do they cost?
reference_answer: Brands and prices are not covered. The documents only describe what good dust control looks like (on-tool extraction matched to the tool, Class M or better vacuums, regular maintenance). You would need supplier or manufacturer information.
label_note: out of scope
